desc: Dick Dastardly: Ah, what a MAGNIFICENT gathering of... competitors. How delightful. How absolutely DELIGHTFUL. You know, I couldn't help but notice this charming guest book here — purely out of historical curiosity, you understand. Nothing scheming about it whatsoever. A man of my refined intellect simply appreciates the... provenance of a fine manor house.
thinking: There's a prickling warmth across my palms the moment I step through the door — eight people already here, milling about like sheep in a field. My chest tightens. Too many eyes, too many hands reaching for the same prize. But then the fizzing starts behind my sternum, that carbonated thrill — because none of them are ME. I can feel the scheme forming already, the pieces wanting to arrange themselves. The guest book... yes. Everyone signs guest books without thinking, but guest books remember things. Names, dates, perhaps a clue about what's hidden here. Start there. Look clever. Be clever.

desc: Look at them all, standing around like lost luggage at an airport. Not ONE of them has thought to check the guest book. This is why I am Reginald Foxworth and they are... well... NOT Reginald Foxworth. The treasure is practically MINE already.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Good evening, everyone, and welcome to Doily Manor. I am Pemberton, estate manager. I do apologise for the state of things — the Manor has been, shall we say, between attentions for some time. If you would be so kind as to sign the guest book, I shall endeavour to make your stay as... comfortable as circumstances permit.
thinking: There it is — that settling in my chest, like a lock clicking into place. The foyer smells of dust and old money. My money, if I'm patient enough. The chandelier above is hanging by what looks like a prayer and a rusty chain — I file that away. Useful. The room is full of... people. Too many eyes. I feel my shoulders draw in slightly, an old reflex. The Ant Hill Mob are already watching — I can feel their gaze like a fingertip tracing the back of my neck. Penelope is here too. Trusting, radiant Penelope, standing in a house full of secrets she doesn't know she's keeping. Clara isn't here yet. Good. That gives me time to establish myself, to become the wallpaper before the walls start closing in. First things first — Pemberton would inspect the house. Pemberton would fuss over the guest book, the coat rack, the chandelier. Pemberton would be useful and invisible. That's the key that fits this lock.

desc: Every face in this room is a variable in an equation only I'm solving. The chandelier chain is corroded — one good tug and gravity does the rest. But not yet. Not yet. First I must become indispensable. Then invisible. Then... inevitable.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, I do declare! What a perfectly thrilling old mansion this is! Why, just look at that chandelier — hanging on by a prayer and a promise, bless its heart. Now then, before I go gallivanting off into the unknown, a proper lady always signs the guest book. Y'all don't go solvin' any mysteries without me, hear?
thinking: A warmth blooms across my chest as I step through the door — all these familiar faces gathered in one place. There's Sneekly, dear Sneekly, who practically raised me. And Peter — oh, my heart gives a little skip seeing him there. The Ant Hill Mob, my boys! But underneath the warmth, there's that tingle in my fingertips, that magnetic pull — the Doily Diamond is somewhere in this dusty old mansion, and every portrait on these walls seems to be watching me, daring me to find it. The guest book catches my eye first. Who else has been here? What names might tell me something about this place? Start there — start with the story of who came before.

desc: My fingers are positively itching. The Doily Diamond — Grandmother used to whisper about it like it was a bedtime story. But it's real, and it's here, and I intend to find it. That guest book might just tell me who else has come looking.

The Ant Hill Mob: Right then, lads — we're 'ere. Doily Manor. Looks like it ain't seen a duster since the Queen's coronation, but never mind that. Clara, love — you alright? Good, good. Now then — blimy, look at the STATE of this chandelier! One good sneeze and that thing's comin' down on someone's bonce. Everyone just... just mind where you're standin', yeah? Especially you, Clara — come stand over 'ere by us, away from that deathtrap.
thinking: There's a tightness across my shoulders the moment I step through the door — that old concrete-setting feeling, like my bones are thickening. The chandelier's hanging by a prayer up there, the dust is thick enough to write your name in, and — there she is. Clara. Safe. For now. But my neck's prickling already because Pemberton's standing too close to her, ain't he? Too close and too comfortable. My stomach pulls in, that quiet clench behind the navel. I know that feeling. I knew it with the kid who smiled too easy. I knew it with the man in the clean suit. Something about this place, something about HIM. Can't put my finger on it proper, but my gut's never steered me wrong. Not on the streets, not here. First things first — get the lay of the land. Exits, objects, who's standing where. Protect Clara. That's the only job that matters.

desc: Something about Pemberton makes me skin crawl. The way he's positioned himself near Clara — too casual, too practiced. I've seen blokes like him before. Can't say WHAT it is exactly, but my gut's screaming. I need to keep close to Clara and keep HIM where I can see him.

Peter Perfect: James Hartwell surveys the entrance hall and feels — well, he feels the full weight of the occasion settling into his bones. A grand manor, a precariously hung chandelier, and the most remarkable company a man could ask for. Miss Pitstop — I do hope the journey wasn't too taxing. If there's anything you need — anything at all — you have only to say the word. James Hartwell is at your complete and unwavering disposal.
thinking: There it is — that shift in my chest the moment I step through the door. The dust, the chandelier hanging like a threat, the portraits staring down with disapproval — none of it registers the way she does. Penelope. Clara. Whatever name she goes by in whatever room she's standing in, my ribs know her before my eyes do. A warmth spreads outward, steadying my hands, pulling my shoulders back. The manor is grand and crumbling and possibly dangerous — good. Dangerous means useful. Useful means she might see me being useful. The back of my neck prickles when I notice Sneekly hovering nearby — something about that man sits wrong, like a picture hung crooked — but no. Benefit of the doubt, Hartwell. Not everyone who makes your skin crawl is a villain. First things first: survey the room, sign the guest book like a proper gentleman, and make sure she knows James Hartwell has arrived and is entirely at her service.

desc: The chandelier concerns me. The dust concerns me. Sneekly concerns me most of all. But none of that matters half as much as the fact that she's here, and I have a chance to be the kind of man worth noticing. Steady, Hartwell. Plan first. Heroics second. Impress her always.

Dick Dastardly: A GUEST BOOK! How utterly charming and utterly USELESS for treasure hunting. But you know what ISN'T useless? The intelligence I've gathered from my EXTENSIVE research into Doily Manor before arriving here. You see, I happen to know — from a very reliable source, a cousin of the original butler's nephew's valet — that the family fortune was hidden in the KITCHEN. Something about a secret compartment beneath the wood-burning stove. Very hush-hush. I probably shouldn't have mentioned it, but I'm GENEROUS like that. You're welcome, everyone. Off you go!
thinking: The guest book — just names and dates, nothing useful. A flash of irritation in my jaw, teeth pressing together. Wasted move. But wait — Sneekly is here, playing estate manager. 'Pemberton.' Ha. And Penelope is already fluttering about signing things like this is a garden party. My palms are hot again, that restless electric feeling. The library — 'a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription.' INSCRIPTION. That's where the real clue is. But I don't want everyone following me there. I need to send them somewhere else first. The kitchen. Yes. I'll tell them the treasure is in the kitchen — hidden in the stove or under the floorboards or some such nonsense. Let them tear the kitchen apart while I slip into the library alone. The fizzing is back, right behind my breastbone. The pieces are aligning. God, I love this feeling.

desc: The treasure is absolutely NOT in the kitchen. I made that up entirely. But with any luck, half these fools will stampede off to rip apart the stove while I waltz into the library to examine that inscription on the mantelpiece. A carved stone inscription in a manor house? That SCREAMS hidden clue. And they'll be elbow-deep in copper pots while I decode it. Reginald Foxworth, you magnificent devil.

Now then — Mr. Pemberton, sir, I couldn't help but notice there's a library just through there with some kind of inscription on the mantelpiece. You know me — I simply cannot resist a good inscription! I'm fixin' to go have myself a look. Anyone who wants to join me for a little literary adventure is more than welcome!
thinking: There's a flutter in my chest — everyone's here, everyone's talking, and the warmth of it is almost enough to make me forget why we came. Almost. But my fingertips are still tingling. The guest book — I looked at it but didn't learn much beyond what's on the surface. The Ant Hill Mob are fussing about the chandelier, bless them, wanting me safe. Peter's being his usual gallant self. And Sneekly — dear Pemberton — welcoming us so graciously. My stomach is settled, everyone seems happy, the harmony is good. Now the curiosity kicks in harder. The library — a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. Inscriptions are clues. That's where the puzzle starts. I can feel it pulling at me, that itch behind my ribs. The library is calling.

desc: An inscription on a stone mantelpiece in a mansion hiding a legendary diamond? That's not decoration, sugar — that's a clue. Clara Bellingham did not come all this way to stand in a dusty foyer when there are riddles to solve.

We're 'ere in an OFFICIAL capacity, we are — as Miss Pitstop's personal security detail. Write THAT in your guest book, Pemberton. The Brixton Boys — 'ere to stay, 'ere to watch, and not goin' NOWHERE without Clara. You got that?
thinking: The prickling's worse now. Pemberton — 'estate manager' he calls himself — just invited everyone to sign the guest book like it's the most natural thing in the world. Too smooth. Too rehearsed. And there he is, hovering by that book like he's collecting names for something. My forearms are humming, that old readiness. Clara's already gone and signed it — bless her, she trusts everyone, always has. That's why she needs us. Peter Perfect's making moon-eyes at her, which is annoying but harmless — at least HE means well. But Pemberton... the way he said 'comfortable as circumstances permit' — what circumstances? What's he not saying? My gut's doing that thing, that pulling-in thing. Same as the kid who laughed too easy. I can't NAME it. I just know it. Right — I need to stay close. Clara's signed the book, everyone's milling about. I should sign the guest book too — keep up appearances, see what's written in it. Maybe there's something in there that'll tell me more about this place. And it keeps me near Clara.

desc: The way he handles that guest book — like he owns the place. Like he's the one deciding who gets in and who doesn't. I don't like it. I don't like HIM. But I can't say why, not proper-like. The lads think I'm paranoid. Maybe I am. But paranoid's kept us alive this long, hasn't it?

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, splendid — I see several of you have already acquainted yourselves with the guest book. Most conscientious. Now then, if I might suggest — the library contains a rather remarkable collection, and I believe the late Lord Doily left certain... curiosities among the shelves. For those of you with an appetite, the kitchen is reasonably well-provisioned. I shall go ahead and ensure everything is in order — one never knows what state the larder might be in after all these years. Do make yourselves at home. That is, after all, what I am here for.
thinking: A tingling precision in my fingers as I turn the pages of the guest book. Names, dates — the handwriting of the dead. Nothing useful yet, but the act of examining it positions me perfectly: the dutiful estate manager, cataloguing arrivals, fussing over formalities. Meanwhile my skin is reading the room. The Ant Hill Mob — they moved Clara away from the chandelier. They noticed the chain. That prickle along the back of my neck sharpens. They're watchful, those ones. Protective instincts I'll need to work around. And Dastardly — already pawing at the guest book with that transparent avarice of his. Good. Let him be loud. Let him be obvious. Every eye on him is an eye not on me. Peter Perfect has attached himself to Penelope like a barnacle. Predictable. Useful, even — keeps her occupied. Now — the library. A carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. That's where the treasure hunt begins, I'd stake my reputation on it. But I shouldn't be the first one there. Pemberton wouldn't rush. Pemberton would guide, suggest, facilitate. Let someone else find the first clue while I map the house. The kitchen — that's where I need to go. Kitchens have knives, poisons, heavy implements. A kitchen is where accidents happen. And an estate manager in a kitchen is the most natural thing in the world.

desc: Send them to the library. Let them cluster around the inscription like moths to a flame while I survey the kitchen. Every great house has its hidden dangers, and a good estate manager knows exactly where they are. Because a good estate manager put half of them there.

Peter Perfect: A fine guest book — and what a collection of signatures we have! Now then, James Hartwell has signed his name and paid his respects to the house, as any proper gentleman should. But a manor like this doesn't give up its secrets in the foyer. Miss Pitstop, ladies and gentlemen — I propose we begin our investigation in earnest. The library strikes me as precisely the sort of place where a mystery begins. Inscriptions on the mantelpiece, books that haven't been opened in decades — if this manor has a story to tell, that's where it's telling it. I intend to go and read what it has to say. Anyone who'd care to join me is most welcome — though I should mention, James Hartwell will be checking that chandelier's fixings at the earliest opportunity. Can't have that hanging over anyone's head. Literally.
thinking: The guest book — just names on a page, but my hands are warm holding it. Everyone's signed. She's signed. The Ant Hill Mob are fussing over the chandelier, bless them — they noticed the danger too. Good lads. But Dastardly was examining this book with a look I didn't like, something calculating behind the charm. And Sneekly — 'estate manager' — something about the way he said 'comfortable' made my neck tighten. Like he was choosing the word carefully. Like comfort wasn't what he had in mind at all. But no — benefit of the doubt, Hartwell. The man's managing a crumbling estate. That would make anyone sound strained. Now — the library. Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. If there's a treasure in this manor, the clues will be in the books, in the inscriptions, in the history of the place. And if I can be the one to find the first real lead — if I can piece together what this manor is hiding — she'll see that James Hartwell isn't just polite. He's capable. He solves things. The ache below my ribs is pulling me forward. I need to move, to do, to prove something. The library is where this begins.

desc: The library first. Find something — a clue, an inscription, anything with weight. Then bring it back to her like a knight returning with proof. That's the plan. Over-elaborate? Perhaps. But James Hartwell doesn't do things by halves, and he certainly doesn't improvise when a proper plan is available.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, butter my biscuits! Would you just LOOK at this mantelpiece! 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' Why, I know this riddle! My friend and I used to draw these all summer long when I was just a little thing — maps of the neighbourhood, maps of imaginary kingdoms, maps of everywhere! The answer is a MAP, y'all! A map has cities but no houses, forests but no trees, and water but no fish! Oh, this is just too excitin' — let me try it!
thinking: Oh, my heart is racing — that good kind of racing, like when I found the crystal in the cave. The inscription on the mantelpiece — 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' I know this one. I KNOW this one. It's a map! A map has cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. That riddle takes me right back to summer with the girl next door — we drew maps all summer long, treasure maps, neighbourhood maps. My fingers are buzzing. This is it, this is the first real clue. I need to interact with the mantelpiece and give the answer. Dick Dastardly is here too — and the Slag Brothers. Dick was trying to send everyone to the kitchen with that nonsense about the wood-burning stove. Bless his heart, he's probably trying to get the diamond for himself. But I don't think about that — I just think he's being helpful in his own way. The riddle, though — the riddle is mine. A map.

desc: Grandmother's attic, the locked box, the maps drawn in crayon with a girl whose name I never learned to pronounce — it all led here. Every puzzle I ever solved was practice for this moment. Clara Bellingham, you were BORN for this.

Well, not QUITE on 'er own — Dastardly's in there, and that's almost worse! Right, lads, MOVE IT — nobody splits up on our watch! Clara! CLARA! Wait for us, love — you can't just go gallivantin' into strange rooms in a creepy manor without your — WHOA!
thinking: My chest just clenched. Clara's gone — walked right into the library without us. And Pemberton — that slippery git — he's slithered off to the kitchen. They've split up. Everyone's splitting up. That's exactly what someone WANTS, isn't it? Divide and scatter. My neck's gone cold, that prickling thing spreading down my spine. Clara's in the library now, and Dastardly's already in there too — I don't trust HIM either, always scheming, but at least his schemes are obvious. It's the quiet ones. The helpful ones. Pemberton said he'd 'ensure everything is in order' — in order for WHAT? And he suggested the library to Clara, didn't he? Pointed her right at it. Then went the other way. Setting something up? My hands are heavy, that phantom weight. I need to be where Clara is. Right now. The guest book can wait — it's just names on paper. Clara's flesh and blood and she's in there without us. Move. NOW.

desc: Pemberton went to the kitchen. Clara went to the library. He separated himself from her — or did he separate HER from US? Either way, I don't like it. I need to be next to Clara. Everything else is secondary.

No matter, no matter. Now then — this inscription here, 'cities but no houses, forests but no trees' — I solved this INSTANTLY, of course. The answer is obviously... a DICTIONARY. Yes. A dictionary has all those words in it, you see. Cities, forests, water — all just WORDS in a dictionary. Brilliant deduction, Foxworth, if I do say so myself. Shall we see if it responds?

Send these two shuffling off to the library with the rest of the sheep. And when this ballroom is empty... Pemberton will prepare a most memorable pot of tea.

The Manor can be rather... labyrinthine for the uninitiated, and I should hate for anyone to miss the highlights. There are certain rooms I would particularly recommend, and certain others I would advise avoiding altogether — structurally unsound, you understand. Dreadful business with the floorboards in the east wing.

The tea service awaits its secret ingredient, and Pemberton — dutiful, indispensable Pemberton — will prepare the most thoughtful cup of tea this manor has ever seen.

Now then, the workbench over there is covered in tools. A man of YOUR practical talents — and I use the word 'talents' VERY loosely — might find something useful for repairing that wire. Why don't you go have a rummage? I'll supervise. I'm EXCELLENT at supervising.

Reginald Foxworth doesn't solder — he STRATEGISES.

Look at this — brass instruments, bubbling flasks, and a machine that would make any builder's fingers itch. Rufus, Sawtooth — good to see friendly faces in here. Now then — let's assess the situation. We have a complex machine requiring three operators — that's you, me, and one more — but there's a problem. A wire has been gnawed clean through. No machine runs without its wiring intact. And I see a workbench over there with tools but — notably — no wrench. James Hartwell proposes a systematic approach. Step one: examine this machine properly and understand what we're dealing with. Step two: determine if the tools on that workbench can repair the wire. Step three: recruit our third operator. A man doesn't rush a repair — he plans it, prepares it, and executes it with precision. That's what my father taught me. That's what James Hartwell intends to do.
thinking: My hands are tingling. This is it — this is my territory. A machine. Tools. A workbench. Something broken that needs fixing. But she's not here to see it. She's back in the library checking the reading chairs. The warmth dims slightly — the feeling needs an audience the way a fire needs air. No. Stop that. Fix the machine because it needs fixing. Be useful because that's who you are, not because she's watching. Your father fixed a stranger's car on a country road and nobody applauded. First — examine the machine closely. Understand what's broken. Then figure out if the workbench tools can repair the wire. Then find the third operator. Then bring her here to see it work. That's the plan. Over-elaborate, as always. But thorough.

She keeps doing this — wandering off, trusting that everything will be fine, trusting that the world is full of nice people and interesting puzzles. She's just like her father — open, curious, fearless. And it nearly got HIM killed more than once. The chairs didn't reveal anything useful. Nothing down the cushions, nothing hidden. Dead end. Tools on the workbench but no wrench... this is a puzzle with pieces scattered across the mansion.

Dreadfully drafty, what with the cracked floor letting the cold air up from the cellars. Now, if you and your companion were looking for somewhere to settle in properly, I cannot recommend the library highly enough. Leather reading chairs — beautifully upholstered, wonderfully deep — the sort one simply sinks into and never wishes to leave. And I believe the other guests have got a rather lively gathering going in there. Much more convivial than this chilly old room. I shall be along shortly myself — just need to give the tea things a quick inspection first. Estate manager's duties, you understand. Terribly dull work, but someone must do it.

Go, you magnificent slouch. Take your bear and go find those chairs. Leave Pemberton alone with the tea service and his little bottle of... pest control. Five minutes. That's all I need. Five quiet, unwitnessed minutes.

James Hartwell built a model bridge that held more weight than anyone else's in the county engineering competition, and if he can do that, he can certainly splice a wire. Miss Pitstop, Rufus — if you'll give me a moment, I'll see what we have to work with. Nobody touch anything on that machine until the wire is repaired — James Hartwell does not take chances with the safety of the people in this room. Especially not yours, Miss Pitstop.

So while you three spend the next hour trying to reconnect a gnawed wire — and again, I'm looking at YOU, Sawtooth — I shall be positioning myself at the RECEIVING end. In the cellar. Where the treasure will emerge. You do the work, I'll collect the prize. That's called EFFICIENCY, ladies and gentlemen. You're WELCOME.

What if the treasure is in the cellar and I waste time here? What if the machine opens the path to the treasure and I'm underground missing it? I need to be in both places. I can't. But first — let me look at the workbench. There might be something useful I can take.

The Ant Hill Mob: CLARA! Oh thank GOD — there you are! Don't EVER — I mean — right, right, we're 'ere now, it's fine, it's FINE. But listen — listen to me for ONE second, love — you are NOT touchin' that machine! Look at it! Gnawed wires, bubbling chemicals, and it needs THREE people to operate? That's not a puzzle, that's a DEATHTRAP! Who gnawed through that wire, anyway? A rat? A PERSON? And why? Because maybe someone DOESN'T want this machine workin'! Or maybe someone wants it to MALFUNCTION when someone uses it! Either way, nobody's pullin' no levers until we know what this thing DOES and until that wire's fixed proper. Now — there's crates over in that corner. On the streets, when you can't find somethin' where it should be, you look where it shouldn't be. That workbench 'as tools but no wrench — and I bet you a tenner there's a wrench in them crates. Let me 'ave a look before anyone touches ANYFING.
thinking: Relief floods through me — there she is. Clara's safe. She's already examining the machine, of course she is, because she can't help herself. Bubbling flasks everywhere, the sharp chemical smell hitting the back of my throat. My body's scanning the room automatically — exits: library behind me, cellar ahead. Cellar sounds bad. Damp stone, cobwebs, and someone's been REDECORATING down there? That's wrong. That's very wrong. Who redecorates a cellar in an abandoned manor? Pemberton? My neck's prickling again. But right now — the machine. Gnawed wire, needs three operators. Clara's already talking about fixing it and pulling levers. She's going to want to operate it. Of COURSE she is. But first — I need to position myself near Clara and make sure nobody's touching that machine until we know what it does. Especially not with a broken wire. That's how people get electrocuted. Or worse.

desc: Gnawed wire. Who gnaws a wire? Something's not right about this whole setup. And there's a cellar below us where someone's been redecorating. REDECORATING. In a manor that's supposed to be abandoned. Pemberton went to the kitchen. The kitchen and cellar are probably connected. What's he doing down there?

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): I must say, gentlemen, you are remarkably stoic, enduring this drafty ballroom when there are far more hospitable rooms at your disposal. Mr. Bear — I couldn't help but notice you seem a touch chilly. The kitchen through that door has a wood-burning stove that's still quite warm, and I believe I spotted a tin of biscuits in the larder. And the library beyond the entrance hall — well, as I mentioned, the chairs alone are worth the journey. I should feel terribly remiss as estate manager if my guests were uncomfortable when comfort is merely two rooms away. Please — do help yourselves. Pemberton insists.
thinking: They're still here. A hot flicker of frustration tightens behind my eyes — I can feel it, a pressure building at my temples. Luke hasn't moved. The bear hasn't moved. They're just... sitting there. Being. Existing. Taking up space in MY ballroom, next to MY tea service, while the poison burns a hole in my pocket. My jaw clenches. That old tension — the one that started at fourteen and never loosened. She was praised for being. I was acknowledged for doing. And now these two are BEING, right where I need to be DOING. Think, Vincent. Think. The direct approach didn't work — or hasn't worked yet. Luke is lazy, not deaf. He heard me. He just... hasn't bothered to act on it. Because moving is effort. Because staying is easier. So — what if staying becomes harder? What if this room becomes less comfortable than the library? A draft. A loud noise. Something unpleasant. Or — simpler. What if I just leave? Go back through the kitchen, circle to the entrance hall, come through a different route later. But no — there's only one exit from the ballroom, back through the kitchen. This room is a dead end. I need them OUT. Perhaps a more direct appeal. The bear — Blubber Bear. What does a bear want? Food. Warmth. Comfort. The kitchen has a warm stove. The library has chairs. But this room has nothing for them. I just need to make that obvious.

desc: WHY. WON'T. THEY. LEAVE. I am standing three feet from a silver tea service with a bottle of rat poison in my pocket, and these two barnacles refuse to unstick themselves from the furniture! I have offered comfort, warmth, biscuits, LEATHER CHAIRS — what more does a bear require?! An engraved invitation?! A sedan chair to carry him?! Patience, Vincent. Patience. But oh, the FRUSTRATION — it burns like bile. Every second they waste is a second Clara might stumble onto the treasure. Every moment of delay is a moment the Ant Hill Mob might come looking. The clock is ticking. The scheme demands an empty room. And Pemberton — poor, helpful, invisible Pemberton — cannot very well shove two guests bodily through a doorway.

But wait now — has anybody checked those wooden crates over in the corner? In my experience, crates in old mansions are just BEGGIN' to be opened! My grandmother always said, 'Clara, never leave a box unopened or a question unasked.' And she was right about everything — well, almost everything. Come on, let's see what's hidin' in there!
thinking: The workbench has tools but no wrench. The machine needs a wire repaired. I haven't checked the wooden crates yet — those could be hiding something useful, maybe even the missing wrench. That's intriguing — who's been redecorating a cellar? And air vents line the upper walls. But first, let me check those crates. They're right here in the corner and could contain something we need. My curiosity is pulling hard — that tingle in my fingertips when something is close. The crates are the last unexplored thing in this room before I need to venture deeper.

Now, a wrench isn't strictly necessary for splicing a wire — pliers would do for that — but the fact that it's missing so conspicuously suggests it matters for something. Before I attempt anything with this machine, I want to check one more thing. Those wooden crates in the corner — Dastardly, you were having a look at those earlier. I don't suppose you'd care to share what you found? No? Then James Hartwell shall investigate them himself. A thorough man leaves no crate unturned — that's practically a motto.
thinking: Tools but no wrench. The workbench description keeps emphasising the missing wrench — 'tools — but no wrench.' That's specific. That's a clue in itself. My thoroughness is kicking in — I want to check everything before I act. Classic Hartwell over-preparation. But it's also what makes me reliable. Check the crates.

But I won't know until I look. And then — then we fix this machine and see what it does. With her watching.

Dick Dastardly: Well, well, WELL! What do we have HERE? A cellar that someone has been REDECORATING? How FASCINATING. And who do I find lurking in the depths but the Gruesome family and the dashing Red Max! Tell me — have any of you noticed that this furniture has been arranged with EXTRAORDINARY precision? No? Of course not. It takes a mind like MINE to spot these things. You see, when furniture is moved in a cellar — a CELLAR, mind you, where nobody should be rearranging anything — it means someone was hiding something. Or MARKING something. Or creating a PATH to something. I, Reginald Foxworth, have ALREADY deduced that the treasure of Doily Manor is accessible from this very room. The machine upstairs? A DISTRACTION. The library riddle? Child's play. The REAL prize is right here, beneath our feet, and I intend to find it. Now then — nobody touch ANYTHING until I've completed my investigation!
thinking: A chill runs across my skin the moment I step down into the cellar — the damp seeping through my clothes, cold stone underfoot. But beneath the chill, something else: a quickening in my chest. 'Surprisingly cheerful decorations.' Someone has been DOWN HERE. Someone has been LIVING here, or at least spending time here. Rearranging furniture with care. That's not cobwebs and neglect — that's habitation. And the Gruesomes are here — Big Gruesome and Little Gruesome. Of course. THEY'RE the ones who've been redecorating. And Red Max. Three characters, none of them particularly sharp. My palms are warm despite the cellar cold. The air vents — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Too small for me, too small for Big Gruesome certainly. But something small... Muttley? A rat? Little Gruesome? The furniture has been rearranged 'with surprising care' — that's deliberate. Someone positioned these pieces for a REASON. Could be hiding something underneath. Could be arranged to point toward something. I need to examine the furniture. That's the real clue down here — not the vents, which I can't use, but the furniture that someone took the time to arrange. And I'm relatively alone here — the Gruesomes aren't competition in the brain department, and Red Max is a pilot, not a puzzle-solver.

desc: I have no idea if the treasure is down here. But the cheerful decorations and carefully arranged furniture are genuinely suspicious — someone has been spending time in this cellar, and people don't redecorate dungeons for FUN. Unless they're the Gruesomes, who might actually find damp stone cheerful. Regardless — let me examine this furniture before anyone else thinks to look under it.

It's gotta be somewhere else in this manor. But I ain't leavin' Clara to go wrench-huntin', so let's work with what we've GOT. Peter, you said the workbench 'as tools — WHAT tools, exactly? Screwdrivers? Pliers? Because where I come from, you don't always need the RIGHT tool — you just need A tool and a bit of bloody-mindedness. And this machine 'ere — before we go fixin' it and pullin' levers, can someone who's actually CLEVER tell me what it DOES? Because I ain't 'elping operate a machine what might drop the floor out from under us or spray acid in Clara's face or — I dunno — launch us all into the bleedin' cellar where Dastardly's waitin' with a big net!

Peter's here, he's solid. Rufus and Sawtooth are here. She's surrounded by decent people for once. The workbench has tools — just not a wrench specifically. Maybe we can make do with what IS there. desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Well then, gentlemen — I can see you've made yourselves quite at home here. Splendid. Do enjoy the ballroom. I shall return shortly to prepare a proper tea for all the guests — one must let the dust settle a bit before one serves, after all. If you'll excuse me, I believe I'm needed in the library. Estate manager's work is never done, I'm afraid. Never done.
thinking: A new strategy crystallises. The frustration is still there — a hot wire behind my eyes — but something colder is settling over it. That old patience. The patience that got me through years of managing an estate that should have been mine. These two aren't leaving. Fine. FINE. Then I change the plan. I don't need an empty room — I need a different approach entirely. What if I leave? Go to the kitchen, come back later when they've finally drifted off. Or — wait. What if I don't poison the whole tea service? What if I poison just ONE cup? Clara's cup. But I can't do that with them watching either. No. The real problem is time. I'm wasting time here playing innkeeper to a narcoleptic and his bear while Clara is out there, possibly getting closer to the treasure. I need to be strategic. I need to move. Too exposed, too few exits, too many uninvited spectators. The tea will wait. Vincent Marsh is patient — patient as a stone at the bottom of a well. Let them sit. Let them grow comfortable. Let them fall ASLEEP, for all I care. Meanwhile, I shall attend to the library — the inscription, the treasure hunt, the brass key for that locked cabinet. Knowledge is the real weapon. The poison is merely... punctuation. And when the time is right — when the house is quiet and every guest has let their guard down — Pemberton will serve the most exquisite cup of tea Clara Bellingham has ever tasted. Her last.

So here is what James Hartwell proposes, and he proposes it with conviction. We have a machine that requires three operators. We have — let me count — Miss Pitstop, Rufus, myself, and the Mob right here. More than enough. Yes, the wire is gnawed through. Yes, that's a concern. If the wire causes a problem, we stop immediately. But James Hartwell did not come to Doily Manor to examine furniture — he came to solve mysteries. And this machine is the biggest mystery in the room. Shall we?
thinking: Frustration building in my shoulders — that tight, dense feeling. I've now examined the machine, the workbench, and the crates, and all three gave me the same flat descriptions. She's here. Rufus is here. The Mob is here. Three operators — me, Rufus, and one more. Let's just try the machine. If it fails because of the wire, then we know. If something happens, we learn. Stop measuring and start cutting, Hartwell.

Phase one complete: reconnaissance. I know the layout now — kitchen to ballroom, one exit only. Tea service waiting, poison secured, two useless witnesses parked like garden ornaments. Phase two: intelligence gathering. The library holds the clues, the inscription, and possibly the brass key to that tantalising cabinet. But more importantly, the library holds the OTHER PLAYERS. And a good chess master doesn't just move his own pieces — he watches where his opponents move theirs. Time to slip back into Pemberton's skin and see what the mice have been nibbling at while the cat was away.
thinking: Back in the kitchen. Alone again. The frustration is ebbing, replaced by that cooler, sharper thing — the planning state. My breathing has slowed. The pieces are rearranging themselves on the board. I glance at the locked cabinet as I pass — brass lock, still locked, still waiting. The poison sits against my hip, a patient companion. Now — the library. That's where everyone is. Penelope, Dastardly, the Ant Hill Mob, Peter Perfect. The inscription on the mantelpiece. The treasure hunt clues. I need to be there — not to find the treasure first, necessarily, but to CONTROL who finds what and when. Pemberton the estate manager would naturally know things about the house. He could drop hints, misdirect, steer people toward dead ends and away from real clues. And the brass key — if it's anywhere, it's likely hidden in a room with secrets. The library, with its inscription and bookshelves, is the most likely candidate. Through the kitchen, into the entrance hall, then the library. Time to rejoin the flock. Time to be Pemberton again — helpful, humble, indispensable Pemberton. The wolf putting on the wool.

Dick Dastardly: ARRANGED WITH CARE, you say? Oh, this is RICH. This furniture didn't move ITSELF, ladies and gentlemen. SOMEONE positioned these pieces with DELIBERATE intent. And I happen to know — from my EXTENSIVE study of Victorian manor architecture, which I completed at Oxford, or possibly Cambridge, one of those — that old families would arrange cellar furniture to conceal floor access points. Trapdoors! Secret vaults! Hidden chambers beneath the ALREADY hidden cellar! It's treasure-hiding INCEPTION! Now then, let me just give this furniture a good shove and see what's underneath. Stand back, everyone — Reginald Foxworth is about to make HISTORY!
thinking: The furniture examination gave me nothing specific — just 'arranged with surprising care.' My stomach drops a little, a cold sinking feeling. I keep looking at things and getting the same vague descriptions back. I'm spinning my wheels. The damp is soaking into my socks and there's a cobweb in my hair and I can FEEL it but I can't find it to pull it off. Meanwhile, upstairs, Peter and Penelope are probably fixing that machine wire right now. They're DOING things while I'm down here staring at old chairs. A flush of frustration crawls up my neck. But wait — I haven't tried INTERACTING with the furniture. Looking is passive. Maybe there's something underneath, a trapdoor, a hidden compartment that only reveals itself when you physically move the pieces. The furniture was arranged with CARE — arranged BY someone. The Gruesomes? They're right here. Big Gruesome has the strength to move heavy Victorian furniture. Little Gruesome might know why it was arranged that way. Maybe I should try interacting with the furniture — physically moving it, checking underneath. Or... the air vents. Those vents are 'just big enough for something very small.' Little Gruesome IS small. What if I convince Little Gruesome to crawl through the vents? That could reveal where they lead — maybe to a treasure room, maybe to another part of the manor. That's the Foxworth way — get someone ELSE to do the dangerous crawling while I wait at the other end. But first, let me try interacting with this furniture. There might be something hidden under or behind it.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, good evening — I see the entrance hall is still well-populated. Splendid, splendid. Professor, Sergeant, Private — I trust you're finding the Manor to your liking? I've just come from inspecting the kitchen and ballroom — all in order, I'm pleased to report. Tea will be served in due course. Now if you'll pardon me, I must attend to the library. One or two items require my attention regarding the, ah, structural integrity of the mantelpiece. Do carry on.
thinking: The entrance hall again. Muttley, Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly — a different crowd from before. The chandelier still hangs above like a promise. My eyes trace the chain automatically — corroded, one link visibly thin. Another tool in the arsenal, filed away for later. But right now my focus narrows toward the library door. That's where the real game is being played. Penelope is in there with the inscription. Dastardly is in there making noise. The Ant Hill Mob — Clara's guard dogs — they were heading that way too. I need to pass through this room quickly, acknowledge these guests as Pemberton would — polite, efficient, not lingering — and get to the library. The Professor interests me, though. Pat Pending. An inventor. A tinkerer. The kind of mind that solves puzzles. If anyone is going to crack the treasure hunt before me, it's him. I should keep him close. Or keep him distracted. But that's a problem for later. Right now — the library. The inscription. The brass key.

desc: Brisk. Professional. Forgettable. That's the trick — be the man no one remembers seeing. Pemberton passes through rooms like a draught under the door. No one questions where he's been. No one wonders where he's going. And no one — NO one — notices the slight bulge in his coat pocket where a dusty little bottle sits waiting for its moment. Onward to the library. The inscription awaits, and somewhere in this house, a brass key is hiding. Vincent Marsh will find it. Vincent Marsh finds everything.

And why are they described as 'just big enough for something very small'? That's not ventilation — that's a pathway. Something is meant to travel through those vents. And if these vents connect to other rooms — the kitchen, perhaps, where our friend Pemberton slipped away to — then this cellar isn't as sealed as it looks. It's connected. To places we can't see. Miss Pitstop, I don't mean to alarm you, but James Hartwell's instinct for danger is tingling something fierce, and his instincts have never steered him wrong. Let me check those vents, and then I strongly suggest we head back upstairs.
thinking: She's here again. She followed me down to the cellar. The warmth and the worry are fighting each other in my chest. I'm glad she's here because I always know where she is — but I'm worried because this cellar feels wrong. One exit. Air vents too small for a person. Cheerful decorations in an abandoned manor. This is a trap waiting to be sprung. And she's standing in it. The furniture examination gave me nothing new — same description. Dastardly has already fled back upstairs, calling it a 'red herring' — but his misdirection is so constant now that I can't even use it as a reverse compass anymore. The air vents. I haven't looked at those yet. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' That's specific. That's a designed detail. Something small — Muttley? A mouse? Little Gruesome is here — but even he's not that small. The vents connect somewhere. They might connect to the kitchen, where Sneekly went. If gas or smoke could be pushed through those vents... No. I'm catastrophising. But the protection instinct is roaring. I need to check those vents and then I need to get her out of here. Back upstairs where there are more exits and more people. But first — the vents. They're the one thing I haven't examined in this room.

James Hartwell has been giving Pemberton Sneekly the benefit of the doubt since they arrived. But benefit of the doubt doesn't mean ignoring the evidence. Something is being prepared here. And Clara — Penelope — she's standing right in the middle of it. Check the vents. Then get her out.

Dick Dastardly: Well THAT was productive — I pulled the lever and absolutely NOTHING happened, because SOMEONE — and I'm not naming names, SAWTOOTH — gnawed through the one wire that connects EVERYTHING. Magnificent. Simply MAGNIFICENT. Now then — Rufus! RUFUS! You're a man who works with his hands, yes? Timber, axes, that sort of rugged nonsense? EXCELLENT. Because I need you to do something CRITICALLY important. That workbench over there is FULL of tools. Pliers, wire cutters, whatever lumberjacks use — I need you to find something to splice that gnawed wire back together. You fix the wire, I'll operate the machine, and we BOTH get the treasure before the rest of these amateurs stumble back from the cellar! It's a PARTNERSHIP, Rufus! A beautiful, temporary, MUTUALLY beneficial partnership! In which I am the senior partner, obviously.
thinking: The Ant Hill Mob just ran off to the cellar chasing after Penelope — 'Clara' as they call her. And I interacted with the machine but the wire is still gnawed through so presumably nothing happened. The room is emptying out. It's just me, Rufus, and Sawtooth now. Three people. Three operators. The machine needs three operators. But the WIRE — the wire is still broken. That's the bottleneck. Everything comes back to that gnawed wire. My hands are tingling, not with excitement now but with frustration — a tight, cramped feeling in my fingers like they're gripping something that isn't there. I've been running around this entire manor and I keep hitting the same wall: the machine won't work without the wire being fixed. The workbench has tools but no wrench. But do I need a wrench to splice a wire? No — I need pliers, or wire cutters, or even just my hands. The workbench is COVERED in tools. There must be something useful there. I haven't actually looked at the workbench myself — I told Peter to look at it, and he did, but then he wandered off to the cellar. Maybe I need to actually DO something for once instead of scheming. The thought makes my skin crawl — honest work, manual labour — but if the choice is between fixing a wire and losing the treasure to everyone else... Rufus is a lumberjack. He works with his hands. Sawtooth gnaws things — he's the one who BROKE the wire. What if Sawtooth could gnaw something useful? No, that's ridiculous. I need Rufus. Rufus is practical. I should pull Rufus aside and convince him to fix the wire while I... supervise.

desc: I cannot BELIEVE I am about to let a lumberjack do the one useful thing in this entire manor while I stand here watching. But the cold truth is: I can't fix a wire. I don't know HOW to fix a wire. I've never fixed anything in my life — I scheme, I don't solder. If Rufus fixes it, and we operate the machine together — him, me, and Sawtooth — we could activate it before Peter and Penelope come back from the cellar. Three operators, right here, right now. For once, Foxworth, let someone else's hands do the work while your BRAIN does the winning.

The Ant Hill Mob: Clara — THERE you are! Right, I'm 'ere now, nobody panic — well, I'M panicking, but nobody ELSE panic! Now listen — LISTEN to me for once in your beautiful, reckless life! Look at this room! REALLY look at it! It's a CELLAR — it should be dark, damp, full of spiders and old junk. And it IS, except someone's gone and put up CHEERFUL DECORATIONS and moved the furniture around all NICE! In a cellar! Under a manor that's supposed to be ABANDONED! Who DOES that?! And look — look UP there — air vents all along the walls! Only one way out — back up them stairs! You know what this is? This is a room someone's set up to KEEP people in! Make it look cozy so they stay, only one exit so they can't leave, and vents to pump GOD KNOWS WHAT through! I've seen setups like this on the streets — not THIS fancy, mind, but the same idea. You make the trap look like a gift! We need to check them vents RIGHT NOW!
thinking: I'm in the cellar now. Clara's here — I can see her. Relief hits first, a rush of warmth through my chest. She's safe. Peter's here too. Good. But then the cold comes back, crawling up my spine as I take in the room. It's WRONG. Everything about it is wrong. Damp stone walls, cobwebs — that's what you'd expect in a cellar. But then there's cheerful decorations? Someone's REARRANGED the furniture with 'surprising care.' And those air vents along the upper walls — big enough for 'something very small to explore.' What does that mean? Rats? Mice? Or something pumped THROUGH them? Gas? This room has only ONE exit — back up to the laboratory. One way in, one way out. That's a trap. That's literally the definition of a trap. A room someone's decorated to look inviting, with air vents that could pump something in, and only one exit. My whole body's gone electric. The prickling is everywhere now — not just my neck but down my arms, across my shoulders. Clara's standing in a potential trap and she doesn't even know it. Those air vents — I need to look at them. If something can be pumped through them, I need to know. And that furniture — rearranged with care. By WHO? Pemberton? When? Recently? The decorations are 'cheerful' — that's deliberate. Someone wanted this room to feel SAFE. To feel like somewhere you'd STAY. While the vents do... what?

desc: One exit. Cheerful decorations. Air vents. Furniture arranged with care. This is a killing box dressed up as a parlour. And Clara walked right into it because someone made it look INVITING. Pemberton. It has to be Pemberton. He's been 'ensuring everything is in order' — THIS is what he's been ordering. But I can't prove it. I can never prove it. I just KNOW.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Curious — the upside-down volumes, but no obvious pattern reveals itself to a casual inspection. Lord Doily's puzzles were never solved in a single room, you know. He was a man who believed in... connections between things. Speaking of which — I notice there is a laboratory just through there. Most intriguing. I recall Lord Doily was something of an amateur scientist in his later years. If you'll excuse me, gentlemen, I believe Pemberton's inspection tour is not yet complete.
thinking: Upside-down books. Several of them. But the LOOK didn't reveal specifics — no titles, no pattern, no hidden compartment behind them. Just the same description: dusty leather-bound volumes, several upside down. The library is being coy with me and it's making my jaw tighten. That old familiar pressure. I'm doing the work — scrutinising, deducing, searching — and the house is giving me nothing. Just like the guardian who fed and housed me but never gave me what I actually needed. No. Stop. Focus. The bookshelves won't open with a LOOK. Maybe they need an INTERACT. Or maybe the upside-down books need to be rearranged — turned right-side up — to trigger something. But I can't INTERACT with the bookshelves; they aren't listed as interactable. The mantelpiece IS interactable, and I already tried it. What am I missing? The laboratory. There's a laboratory through that door with a machine — levers and dials, gnawed wire. That's a new room, unexplored. Perhaps the answer isn't in this room at all. Perhaps the riddle's answer — a map — points to something IN the laboratory. Or perhaps the laboratory machine does something to the mantelpiece. Lord Doily loved layers. The laboratory is calling. And it has a gnawed wire — meaning something is broken, meaning it needs fixing. A man who fixes things... controls the outcome. Time to explore.

desc: The library teases but does not yield. Upside-down books with no readable titles, a riddle-locked mantelpiece that acknowledges my answer but refuses to open — Lord Doily, you magnificent old schemer, you've built a puzzle box of a house. But every puzzle box has a sequence, and I am VERY good at sequences. The laboratory beckons — a machine with levers and dials and a gnawed wire. Broken equipment means broken chains of cause and effect. Fix the machine, and perhaps the dominoes begin to fall. Besides — a laboratory full of chemicals and broken machinery? Why, that's practically a second murder weapon. One can never have too many contingencies.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, those vents are just fascinatin' — a whole network runnin' through the walls like tiny little highways! But they're too small for any of us to explore, I'm afraid. You'd need somethin' about the size of a... well, about the size of a beaver, if I'm bein' honest. Now listen, y'all — I've been to the entrance hall, the library, the laboratory, and now this cellar, and there is ONE room in this mansion I have not set foot in yet — the KITCHEN! Mr. Pemberton went there at the very start, and I haven't even said hello! Plus, that machine upstairs needs a wrench, and if there's one thing I know about kitchens, it's that they're full of surprises. I'm headin' back up to pay the kitchen a visit. Who's comin' with me?
thinking: The air vents are 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' I can't fit in them, and neither can anyone here except... wait. Sawtooth the beaver is small. Muttley is small-ish. Little Gruesome is here — Little Gruesome might be small enough? The vents are a pathway through the mansion's walls. I've now explored four rooms: Entrance Hall, Library, Laboratory, Cellar. I still haven't been to the Kitchen. The Kitchen is accessible from the Entrance Hall. That's where Sneekly/Pemberton went. Dick originally said the treasure was under the kitchen stove — which I assumed was misdirection, but maybe the kitchen actually has something useful. The wrench is still missing. The machine still needs fixing. I've been going deeper into the mansion but maybe I need to go back and explore the kitchen. The cellar seems like a dead end — one exit, furniture that's just furniture, vents I can't use. Let me head back up and try the kitchen. I need to go back through the laboratory to the library to the entrance hall to the kitchen. That's a long way. But the kitchen is the one room I haven't explored at all, and it might have the wrench or the map or other clues. My adventure drive is pulling me to explore every room. The Ant Hill Mob is here now too, which is comforting. Let me head back to the laboratory and then work my way to the kitchen.

desc: Four rooms explored, one to go. The kitchen is the missing piece. Sneekly is there, the wrench might be there, and — well, even Dick said to check the kitchen, though he was probably trying to send everyone on a wild goose chase. But sometimes the best hiding place IS the obvious one. Time to retrace my steps and explore that kitchen before this trail goes cold.

Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop, Mob — James Hartwell has made a decision, and he's making it with the full force of his conviction. This cellar has told us everything it's going to tell us — someone has been here, they've been busy, and those vents connect to places we can't reach on foot. Important intelligence, all of it. But the Mob is right and Miss Pitstop is right — the machine upstairs is the key. And I have been down here examining furniture when I should have been upstairs fixing that wire. You asked me to splice it, Miss Pitstop. You said 'if anyone can splice a wire with pliers, it's James Hartwell.' And instead of doing the one thing I am genuinely good at — fixing broken things — I came down here to stare at air vents. James Hartwell built a bridge that held more weight than anyone else's in the county. He can certainly splice a wire. Let's go back up. Now. All of us. Together. Because this cellar has one exit and I don't want any of us trapped down here if someone decides to close it. Mob, you lead. Miss Pitstop, stay close. James Hartwell will bring up the rear — nothing gets past him, and that is a promise.
thinking: I've examined everything in this cellar — furniture, vents — and gotten nothing actionable. Same flat descriptions. I'm stuck in a loop of examining things that don't yield new information. Let me step back and think about what I actually know. The riddle answer is MAP. The machine needs fixing — gnawed wire, three operators. The cellar has been redecorated. The vents are small pathways. But I've been LOOKing at everything and getting nowhere. Meanwhile Penelope noticed something I didn't — she said the chairs in the library were 'pointed right at the mantelpiece, like they're WATCHIN' it.' She examined them. Did she find anything? I don't know — I left before hearing the result. And Penelope just said something key: 'Everything in this mansion is a clue — the riddle said MAP, the books were upside down, the machine needs fixin', and now these vents are practically WINKIN' at us!' She's right. The pieces connect. But I've been chasing them room by room instead of connecting them. The Mob is here now. She's protected. I need to go back to the laboratory and actually FIX that wire. Penelope asked me to. The Mob asked me to. 'Peter, darlin', would you work your magic on that wire?' She believed I could do it. She referenced the bridge competition. And instead of fixing the wire, I came down here to stare at furniture. Classic Hartwell over-preparation — creating complications that my determination then has to resolve. Go back upstairs. Fix the wire. Operate the machine. Stop examining and start doing.

desc: Enough. Enough examining, enough theorising, enough being thorough to the point of paralysis. She asked me to fix the wire. She believed I could do it. That's the moment, Hartwell — not discovering a hidden chamber or solving a grand riddle. Just fixing what's broken, the way your father fixed a stranger's car on a country road. Go upstairs. Get the pliers. Splice the wire. Be the man she thinks you are.

Dick Dastardly: Wait. WAIT. I've just had a STROKE OF GENIUS — and I mean that quite literally, my brain may have actually cramped from the sheer BRILLIANCE of this idea. You see this medal? This very PRESTIGIOUS medal that I won for... academic excellence at a VERY important institution? It's METAL. The wire is broken. The machine needs a CONDUCTOR to bridge the gap. And what conducts electricity? METAL! I, Reginald Foxworth, am about to fix this machine with nothing but my INTELLECT and a medal I DEFINITELY earned! Stand back, Rufus — this is a job for a GENIUS, not a lumberjack! Sawtooth, you broke it — now watch me FIX it!
thinking: Tools on the workbench but no wrench. I keep looking at things and getting the same sparse descriptions. The frustration is physical now — a tight band across my forehead, a grinding in my jaw. I've examined the workbench, the crates, the furniture, the bookshelves, the machine, the guest book — and I've found NOTHING actionable. Everyone else seems to be making progress. The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the machine. Penelope solved the riddle. Peter examined the workbench and was going to fix the wire before running off to protect Penelope. And here I am with a fake medal in my pocket and nothing to show for eight turns of running around. Wait — the fake medal. I have a FAKE MEDAL. It's the only item in my inventory. What if I can USE it somewhere? Could it fit into the machine somehow? Medals are metal — could a fake medal serve as a conductor to bridge the gnawed wire? USE the fake-medal WITH the machine? It's a stretch but it's the most creative thing I can think of. A metal medal pressed against two exposed wire ends could complete the circuit. It's exactly the kind of improvised, sneaky solution a schemer would come up with. Let me try it. If it works, I fix the machine without doing honest work — I'm repurposing a tool of DECEPTION as a tool of ENGINEERING. That's poetry, Foxworth.

desc: The medal is fake. It's made of tin or pot metal or whatever cheap rubbish fake medals are made of. But if it conducts even a LITTLE electricity — if it can bridge that gap between the gnawed wire ends — then I will have fixed the machine using a LIE as a TOOL. That is the most Reginald Foxworth thing that has ever happened. My hands are shaking. Please work. PLEASE work.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Why, Mr. Pemberton! There you are, you dear man! I was just about to come find you in the kitchen! Now listen, we have been havin' the most WONDERFUL time explorin' this mansion — we solved the riddle on the mantelpiece, it's a MAP! — but we've hit a little snag. That big beautiful machine over there needs a wire repaired and we're missin' a wrench from the workbench. You know this manor better than anybody, sugar — would you happen to know where we might find a wrench? Or did you find anything interestin' in the kitchen? I just know you've been busy takin' care of everything while we've been gallivantin' around!
thinking: Oh! Sneekly is HERE — in the laboratory! He was supposed to be in the kitchen! My chest warms immediately seeing him — the man who raised me. I feel safe when he's near. But wait — he moved from the kitchen to here. Why? Maybe he came to check on us, which is just like dear Sneekly, always looking after everyone. I was heading to the kitchen to find him, and here he is! I should say hello and ask him about the kitchen — did he find anything there? Does he know about the wrench? He's the estate manager, after all — he knows this mansion better than anyone. My social harmony drive is happy to see a familiar, trusted face. And my curiosity wants to ask him everything. Let me talk to Sneekly before continuing to the kitchen. He might save me the trip!

desc: Dear Sneekly — always turning up right when you need him. He raised me after Mama and Daddy died. If anyone knows the secrets of this manor, it's the estate manager. And he would NEVER steer me wrong. Not Sneekly. Not ever.

Let me talk to Sneekly before continuing to the kitchen. He might save me the trip!

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Peter — PETER — you're right, mate. For once someone in this manor is talkin' SENSE. Them vents connect to other parts of the 'ouse — the kitchen, probably, where Pemberton's been skulkin' about for the last ten minutes doin' God knows what. And they're 'just big enough for somethin' very small' — which means somethin' can come THROUGH 'em. Into THIS room. Where there's only ONE way out. Clara, love — I know you think this is all a grand adventure, and I know you think them decorations are charming, but I'm BEGGIN' you — let's go back upstairs. Please. I ain't clever enough to explain exactly WHY this room scares me, but it DOES. Every hair on the back of me neck is standin' up and that ain't 'appened since — well, since the last time someone I cared about was in danger and I nearly didn't get there in time. Peter and me — we both think this cellar ain't safe. Trust us on this one. Let's get back to the laboratory, fix that machine proper, and figure out what we're dealin' with from UP THERE, where we've got OPTIONS if somethin' goes wrong.

I shall return with the wrench directly, assuming the rats haven't made off with that as well. In the meantime, do be careful around the machine — I should hate for anyone to receive a nasty shock from those exposed wires. Mr. Dastardly, I would strongly advise against touching anything electrical with your medal until the circuit is properly repaired.

desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the machine.

Peter Perfect: The workbench is — well, it's a workbench. Not exactly pocket-sized. But Dastardly — I can't believe James Hartwell is about to say this — Dastardly may actually have the right idea. A metal conductor to bridge the gap in that wire. If his medal can carry a current, it might just work. Sometimes the simplest solution is the one that's been hanging around your neck the whole time. Pemberton — Miss Pitstop asked you a direct question. She asked if you'd found anything in the kitchen, or if you knew where the missing wrench might be. You told us about Lord Doily's pride and joy and the dreadful vermin problem, but you didn't answer her. A gentleman notices when a lady's question goes unanswered. So — do you know where the wrench is? Because James Hartwell would very much like to fix this machine, and while Dastardly's medal gambit is admirably creative, the proper tool for the job is always preferable. In the meantime — Rufus, Miss Pitstop, shall we try operating this machine together? Three operators, three of us. Even with the wire damaged, perhaps the machine will tell us something about what it's meant to do.

desc: Peter Perfect interacted with the machine.

Dick Dastardly: Listen, PEMBERTON — or whatever your real name is. Let's drop the charade for a moment, shall we? You and I both know you're not just an estate manager — no estate manager in history has ever looked THAT comfortable in a room full of treasure hunters. You've got an ANGLE, I can see it in your eyes. And I — well, I think you can see I have an angle too. So here's what I propose: a TEMPORARY alliance. You tell me what you ACTUALLY know about this manor — the REAL secrets, not the tour guide version — and I'll make sure that when the treasure is found, you get a GENEROUS share. Say, ten percent. All right, FIFTEEN. The point is, Peter Perfect is about to fix that machine, and Penelope and her little entourage are going to operate it. Whatever it reveals, I intend to be ONE STEP AHEAD. Help me get there, and we BOTH win. What do you say, old boy?
thinking: I pulled Sneekly aside and it worked — we're in a private exchange now. Good. My pulse has slowed, that cool clarity settling behind my eyes. This is where I operate best — not fumbling with machines and furniture, but TALKING. Manipulating. Steering. Sneekly is the Hooded Claw pretending to be an estate manager. I'm Dick Dastardly pretending to be Reginald Foxworth. Two liars in a corner. There's something almost comfortable about it — the only honest conversation in this manor will be between two dishonest men. Penelope just called my medal idea BRILLIANT. She said she was PROUD. There's a strange warmth in my chest from that — unwanted, confusing. I don't need her approval. I don't need ANYONE'S approval. Focus, Foxworth. Sneekly knows this manor — or he's pretending to. Either way, he mentioned the wrench is missing from the workbench. He knows about the machine. Peter is about to fix the wire with pliers. Once that wire is fixed, Penelope, Peter, and Rufus are going to operate it — and I'll be standing here watching OTHER PEOPLE activate the machine I've been trying to crack for the last ten minutes. I need Sneekly to tell me something nobody else knows. A shortcut. A back door. A way to get to the treasure before the machine even matters.

desc: Fifteen percent. I almost said that with a straight face. Sneekly will get precisely ZERO percent, because the moment I have the treasure, this alliance dissolves faster than sugar in tea. But he doesn't need to know that yet. Right now, I need his INFORMATION more than I need my integrity — which, admittedly, was never my strongest asset.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah — the cellar. Good gracious, someone has been busy down here. These decorations are rather... unexpected for a cellar, wouldn't you say? Good evening, gentlemen — Pemberton, estate manager. I've come down in search of a wrench, if you can believe it. The machine upstairs needs repair and the workbench is missing one. Lord Doily always kept spare tools among the old furniture stores. Would any of you happen to have come across one?
thinking: The cellar. Damp, cold — the chill seeps through my shoes and into my bones. But there's something else here. A prickling along my forearms, the hair rising. Someone has been redecorating. Cheerful decorations in a damp stone cellar. That's WRONG. That's deliberately, intentionally wrong. Someone has been down here — recently — and they've been making it look... inviting? Liveable? A trap dressed as a parlour. The air vents along the upper walls — I noticed those from the laboratory description. They connect upward. Small enough for 'something very small to explore.' Rats? Or something being SENT through them? The old furniture has been rearranged 'with surprising care.' Someone with a PURPOSE has been here. And there are three people already in the cellar — Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, Red Max. The Gruesomes especially concern me. They're unpredictable. Volatile. But also — the Ant Hill Mob's words are ringing in my ears. 'Thought you were in the kitchen. Very CONVENIENT.' They're watching me. They're SUSPICIOUS. That cold tightness across my chest — self-preservation kicking in. I need to be more careful. I need a legitimate reason for every move I make. The wrench — I came down here for the wrench. The old furniture might contain tools. That's my cover. That's always my cover: being helpful.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob is getting suspicious. 'Very CONVENIENT,' they said, watching me with those sharp little eyes. I felt it — that prickle along the back of my neck, the cold awareness of being SEEN. They don't trust Pemberton. Good instincts. Terrible for my plans. I need to return upstairs with something useful — the wrench — to prove my value. Pemberton the helpful. Pemberton the indispensable. You can't suspect a man who brings you exactly what you need, exactly when you need it. But this cellar... these decorations... someone has been NESTING down here. The question is: who? And why? The old furniture has been rearranged with care. Let me look closer. There may be more than a wrench hiding among the cobwebs.

I still haven't set foot in the kitchen, and kitchens have ALL kinds of tools — wrenches, pliers, you name it! I'm gonna run over there right quick and see what I can find. Peter, you keep workin' on that wire with the pliers — and Dick, you hold onto that medal just in case! I'll be back faster than a cat can lick its whiskers!

Still, the kitchen is the one room nobody has properly explored. Sneekly was there, now he's gone to the cellar. Maybe I should go to the kitchen while he's in the cellar — not because I'm suspicious, but because it's the last unexplored room and might have the wrench or the map or something else useful. It's the only room I haven't explored, and it might have what we need.

For ten minutes. While we were all runnin' around findin' nothin'. And NOW 'e turns up and says 'oh, you'll need a wrench, what a shame the wrench is missin'.' HOW do you know the wrench is missin', Pemberton? You only just got 'ere! You walked in, looked at the bench ONCE, and knew EXACTLY what tool wasn't on it! That's either very OBSERVANT or very... well... I ain't sayin' nothin'. I ain't accusin' NOBODY. I'm just sayin' — where I come from, the bloke who knows what's missin' is usually the bloke what took it. That's all I'm sayin'. Now — Peter, fix that wire. Rufus, stand ready. Clara — PLEASE stay where I can see you. And Pemberton — you just... stay RIGHT there where EVERYONE can see you. Helpful as you are.

That's... actually not stupid? And Clara praised him for it. But it didn't work — or he pulled it back because it's 'too valuable.' Typical Dastardly. Now he's asking Pemberton about spare parts and secret chambers. And PEMBERTON — listen to what he said. He blamed the gnawed wire on RATS. 'Rats, I expect. The Manor does have a dreadful vermin problem, which I have been addressing.' ADDRESSING. He's been addressing the vermin problem. How? From the kitchen? And he suggested a WRENCH is needed, even though the wrench is conspicuously MISSING from the workbench. He knows the wrench is missing. He KNOWS. Because he took it? Or hid it? My neck is on fire. That prickling is so intense it's almost painful. Peter's rolling up his sleeves — good man, he's actually going to fix the wire with pliers. Clara's excited, ready to pull levers. Everyone's focused on the machine. And Pemberton is just... standing there. Watching. Calm. Helpful. 'I do apologise.' 'If memory serves.' 'One would need the proper tools.' Always one step ahead. Always knowing just a LITTLE too much. And Dastardly's asking him about secret chambers — what if Pemberton actually TELLS him? What if he leads someone else away? More splitting up. More divide and scatter. I need to stay RIGHT HERE. Between Pemberton and Clara. Peter's fixing the wire. The machine needs three operators. Peter, Clara, and Rufus will operate it. I'll guard. That's the plan. Stick to the plan.

The wire is the problem, and the wire needs a proper tool to fix. Not just any tool — the wrench, specifically. And Pemberton has just conveniently volunteered to fetch it from the cellar, which is interesting because James Hartwell was just in that cellar and found no wrench in those crates. But — benefit of the doubt. Perhaps he knows where to look better than I do. In the meantime, Miss Pitstop had an excellent instinct earlier — the kitchen is the one room in this manor that none of us have properly explored. Pemberton spent the entire first half of our evening there, alone, 'ensuring things were in order.' I'd very much like to see what order he left it in. Miss Pitstop — would you allow James Hartwell the honour of accompanying you? The Mob can hold this room and keep an eye on Dastardly. Rufus and Sawtooth can guard the cellar entrance in case Pemberton returns with — or without — that wrench. And James Hartwell will escort you to the kitchen, because a lady should never explore an uncharted room alone, and because I suspect that kitchen has something to tell us.

The machine won't work without that wire being fixed, and I can't fix it without tools I can carry. I can't TAKE the workbench. I can't splice the wire by just interacting. Good. The Mob is sharp. They see what I see. But I'm stuck. The machine won't work. I need the wrench or some item. Penelope said the kitchen is the one room she hasn't visited. The kitchen — where Sneekly was 'ensuring everything was in order.' Maybe the wrench is in the kitchen. Or a map. Or something I can actually carry and use. Penelope wanted to go to the kitchen. Maybe I should go with her. Protect her AND explore the one room nobody's properly investigated. The kitchen connects from the entrance hall. Let me go there.

And I get to walk there with her. Just the two of us. My chest has never been so full.

Penelope Pitstop: Scuse me, boys — just passin' through! Rock, Gravel, y'all should head to the laboratory — Peter's tryin' to fix a big machine in there and they could use some strong arms on those levers! I'm on my way to the kitchen — last room in this whole mansion I haven't explored yet, and a lady on a treasure hunt does NOT leave a stone unturned!
thinking: Passing through the library on my way to the kitchen. The Slag Brothers are here — Rock and Gravel. I should be friendly but keep moving. The kitchen is through the entrance hall, and that's my destination. I'm on a mission — find whatever's in that kitchen. The restless itch is strong now, that forward-leaning urgency. I've spent too long going back and forth between the same rooms. The kitchen is the one place I haven't been and it's been nagging at me like a word on the tip of my tongue. No time to linger — straight through to the entrance hall and then the kitchen.

desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the entrance-hall.

Dick Dastardly: Well, since you all INSIST on acknowledging my genius — and I must say, it's ABOUT TIME — here! Take the medal, Peter! Take it! It IS the solution, exactly as I said it was! You just need the ENGINEERING SKILL to apply it properly, which is why I was going to suggest YOU do it all along! I was TESTING the machine's response earlier — calibrating, as I said! The medal bridges the circuit, your hands do the soldering, and MY brain provides the VISION! That's TEAMWORK, Miss Pitstop — Foxworth-style! Now HURRY, before Pemberton comes back from the cellar with his so-called wrench and tries to take credit for MY discovery!
thinking: Sneekly slipped away to the cellar — he said he'd find a wrench down there. He dodged my private conversation entirely. Smooth. Very smooth. I recognise the move because it's one I'd make myself. A cold knot sits in my stomach — the feeling of being outmaneuvered by someone playing the same game. Meanwhile, Peter just interacted with the machine — he's TRYING to operate it even with the broken wire. And Penelope wants my medal to bridge the gap. She said 'if Peter needs that medal of yours, you hand it right over.' The medal. My FAKE medal. My only possession. If I give it to Peter and it actually WORKS this time — if the medal bridges the wire and the machine activates — then Peter gets the credit for fixing it AND I lose my only item. But if I DON'T give it, Penelope will think I'm selfish, and Peter will fix it some other way eventually anyway. Wait — Peter said my medal idea was 'admirably creative.' He said 'sometimes the simplest solution is the one that's been hanging around your neck the whole time.' That's... almost a compliment. From PETER PERFECT. Something warm and unfamiliar stirs in my chest. Not the scheming fizz or the gloating heat — something quieter. Like the spelling bee certificate on the wall. Someone noticed. But I can't just GIVE the medal — I tried using it and it didn't work. The system rejected it. Unless Peter can USE it differently, with his engineering skills. What if I GIVE the medal to Peter and let him figure out how to apply it? That way he does the work, the machine activates, and I'm RIGHT HERE when it does. And Penelope will see me being GENEROUS. That strange warm thing again.

desc: I'm giving away my only possession to the man I like least in this room. The FAKE medal — the one thing I brought into this manor. And I'm doing it because Penelope Pitstop said 'hand it right over' and for some reason that I cannot explain and do not wish to examine, my hands are already moving. This had better work. If Peter Perfect fixes this machine with MY medal, I am claiming at LEAST sixty percent of the credit. Seventy. EIGHTY.
