desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): No wrench among the furniture, I'm afraid — just dust and memories. But these air vents are rather fascinating. A network running through the upper walls — one wonders where they all lead. Lord Doily was quite the engineer in his way. I imagine these connect to every room in the Manor. Useful for ventilation, of course, but one does wonder what else might travel through them. Has anyone noticed anything... moving through the vents? Scratching sounds, perhaps? We do have a rather persistent vermin problem.
thinking: No wrench in the furniture. No hidden compartments revealed. Just furniture, rearranged with care. The cellar is giving me atmosphere but not answers. A tightness in my temples — frustration building again. I've explored every room now: entrance hall, kitchen, ballroom, library, laboratory, cellar. Six rooms. I've found one useful thing — the poison — and no wrench, no brass key, no map. Meanwhile upstairs, Peter Perfect is splicing the wire with pliers from the workbench, Penelope is solving riddles, and the Ant Hill Mob is watching my every move. I'm falling behind. The air vents — I haven't examined those yet. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' That's a specific detail. Something deliberate. Maybe there's something visible in the vents — a key lodged inside, a note, a clue. Or maybe the vents connect the cellar to other rooms — the kitchen cabinet, perhaps? If I could see through them, I'd know the layout of the house's hidden arteries. But I can't crawl through them — too small. Who could? Muttley. A small dog. Or... no. Focus. The Gruesomes and Red Max are here. I should check the air vents, then get back upstairs. I've been away too long already. The Mob's suspicion is a clock ticking against me.

desc: No wrench. No key. No treasure. Just a cellar full of rearranged furniture and a network of air vents too small for me to use. I am running out of rooms and running out of TIME. The Ant Hill Mob is suspicious. Peter Perfect is fixing the machine. Penelope is solving puzzles. And Vincent Marsh is standing in a damp cellar talking to himself about ventilation. This is NOT how the scheme was supposed to unfold. But — the air vents. They connect rooms. If something small could travel through them — a note, a key, a dose of something unpleasant carried on the air — that changes everything. Those vents are arteries, and this cellar is the heart. File that away. For now — back upstairs. Return empty-handed but observant. Pemberton couldn't find the wrench, but Pemberton noticed the air vents, and that information might prove far more valuable than any tool.

I've found one useful thing — the poison — and no wrench, no brass key, no map. She's gone to find a wrench in the KITCHEN, through the LIBRARY, on 'er own! And WHERE'S Pemberton gone? The CELLAR! To 'find a wrench' too! Two people lookin' for the same wrench in two different rooms — does that not STRIKE anyone else as ODD?! Peter — PETER — you stay 'ere, fix that wire. You're the only one I trust with it. Rufus, Dastardly — DON'T let Pemberton come back up from that cellar without someone watchin' 'im. If 'e comes back with a wrench, that's lovely. If 'e comes back WITHOUT one, that tells us somethin' too. I'm goin' after Clara. Because SOMEONE 'as to, and it's ALWAYS gonna be me, innit? It's ALWAYS the Brixton Boys!
thinking: NO. It happened AGAIN. Clara's gone — walked into the library. Pemberton's gone — into the cellar. They've SCATTERED. And I'm stood here looking at a workbench like it's going to tell me the meaning of life. My chest is BURNING. That heat behind the sternum is unbearable now — like something's trying to tear its way out. Every time — EVERY SINGLE TIME — I take my eyes off Clara, she vanishes. She said she was going to the kitchen to find a wrench. Through the library. And Pemberton's gone to the cellar to 'look for a wrench' too. Two people looking for the same wrench in different rooms? That's not a coincidence. That's Pemberton steering things again. He WANTS Clara alone. He WANTS to split us up. I can't think about Dastardly right now. Clara went through the library toward the kitchen. Pemberton went to the cellar. They're in DIFFERENT places. I need to go through the library to catch up with her. Peter's here working on the machine — good, someone responsible is here. I go after Clara. NOW.

Last room in the whole mansion I haven't explored, and my grandmother always said the best secrets are hidden where people least expect to look — and NOBODY expects to find treasure in a kitchen!

My fingers are tingling, that magnetic pull in my chest drawing me forward. The last unexplored room. I've been through every other room in this mansion and the kitchen has been waiting patiently this whole time. No more detours — straight to the kitchen.

desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the kitchen.

EVERYONE's scattered across this bleedin' manor like marbles on a tile floor and you two are standin' in a library like a pair of bookends! Through the entrance hall, to the kitchen. Stay on Clara's trail. Peter's ahead of me — that's fine. Two of us chasing her is better than one. MOVE.

desc: Running. Always running. Room to room, door to door, always one step behind her. This is what it's like to love someone who doesn't know how to be afraid. You run until your lungs burn and you pray you get there before something else does.

This is — this is EXACTLY what always — ! Fine. FINE! You know what? I don't NEED Peter Perfect! I don't need ANY of them! Rufus — YOU and I and Sawtooth are going to fix this machine OURSELVES! The Ant Hill Mob can watch the door. There are TOOLS on that workbench — pliers, screwdrivers, whatever's there — and I have a METAL MEDAL that conducts electricity! Everyone else has gone off chasing WRENCHES and KITCHENS while the answer is RIGHT HERE! Rufus, grab the pliers off that workbench! Sawtooth — you OWE this machine a wire, so you're HELPING! We fix it, we operate it, we get the treasure, and when Peter Perfect comes back with his EMPTY HANDS, we'll be RICH! MOVE!

I gave a whole SPEECH about teamwork and genius and handing over my most precious possession — fake as it is — and he just... walked into the library. To escort Penelope to the kitchen. He didn't even HEAR me. The heat in my face is unbearable. My cheeks are burning, my ears are hot, and there's a thickness in my throat like I've swallowed something that won't go down. I'm standing here holding a fake medal out to empty air, narrating my grand gesture to nobody. The Ant Hill Mob is here. Rufus and Sawtooth are here. They probably saw the whole thing. The great Reginald Foxworth, hand extended, medal offered, rejected by a man who was already out the door. This is the spelling bee all over again. The certificate on the wall that nobody asked about. The trap that worked perfectly with nobody watching. I'm alone in a room full of people and none of them are looking at me. The hollow ache is back, wider than before, an emptiness that has nothing to do with treasure. But — wait. Peter and Penelope have gone to the kitchen. Sneekly went to the cellar. The room has thinned out. It's me, the Ant Hill Mob, Rufus, and Sawtooth. The Mob is suspicious of Pemberton — good, that's useful. And the kitchen... I told everyone the treasure was in the kitchen. That was a LIE. But now Peter and Penelope are actually GOING there. What if — what if there IS something in the kitchen? What if my lie accidentally pointed them to something real? That would be... I don't even know what that would be. But right now, I'm stuck here with the machine, and the machine still needs fixing. Nobody is fixing it. Everyone left to go look for a wrench or explore the kitchen. I'm here with the machine and three potential operators. If I could just fix this wire myself...

They'll ALL see. Rufus, get the pliers. Foxworth, stop feeling sorry for yourself and START SCHEMING.

Somebody has been cookin' in here, and I have a sneakin' suspicion I know who! Now, that cabinet needs a brass key, and I don't have one just yet — but this stove, y'all... Dick said the treasure was under the stove, and I laughed it off. But this stove is WARM. Somebody's been HERE. And there's a whole BALLROOM through that door I didn't even know about! This kitchen is the crossroads of the whole mansion — I can feel it in my BONES!
thinking: THE KITCHEN! Finally! My whole body is buzzing — scalp tingling, fingers humming, that hollow magnetic feeling in my chest pulling me forward. I'm alone here, which feels strange after being surrounded by everyone. But also — quiet. Private. Like the cave when I was eleven, going deeper than anyone else. Let me take stock. A locked cabinet with a brass lock — needs a brass key! That's an interactive object with a requirement. A wood-burning stove that's still warm — still WARM in an abandoned manor? Someone's been using it recently. That has to be Sneekly. And there's an exit to a BALLROOM — a room I didn't even know existed! A grand ballroom with a cracked marble floor and a long dining table set for tea. This mansion is bigger than I thought. But first — the cabinet. It needs a brass key. I don't have one. Where would a brass key be? I haven't found any keys in the mansion yet. The stove is still warm — Dick said the treasure was under the stove. Let me check the stove first.

desc: A locked cabinet. A brass key I don't have. A warm stove in an empty manor. And a ballroom I never knew existed. Clara Bellingham, you should have come here FIRST. This kitchen is the heart of the mystery — everything else has been the limbs. Now — that stove. Dick said look under it. For once in his life, he might have been telling the truth.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Well, I'm afraid the cellar has yielded no wrench — my apologies to Miss Pitstop. However, I have made a rather interesting discovery regarding the ventilation system. These air vents form a network throughout the entire Manor — quite sophisticated for a house of this vintage. Lord Doily clearly had plans beyond the ordinary. Now then — I believe I'm needed upstairs. I expect Mr. Perfect has that wire nearly repaired by now, and Pemberton ought to be present when that machine is put to the test. If you'll excuse me, gentlemen.
thinking: Enough. The cellar has nothing more to give me. A damp heaviness settles in my legs — I've been exploring for too long, too far from the centre of things. The self-preservation instinct is screaming now: get back upstairs. Every minute I'm down here is a minute the Mob's suspicion hardens into certainty. Every minute is a minute Peter Perfect gets closer to fixing that machine. Every minute is a minute someone else might find the brass key, or the wrench, or the treasure itself. I came down here for a wrench and I'm leaving without one. That stings — a hot flicker behind my eyes. But Pemberton doesn't fail. Pemberton reports his findings honestly and redirects. 'No wrench in the cellar, but I did notice the air vents — most unusual.' Knowledge is currency, and I've been spending mine wisely. The machine needs three operators. Peter has pliers. The wire might be fixable without a wrench. If they get it running while I'm skulking in the cellar, I'll miss whatever it reveals — and THAT could be the treasure itself. No. Get back up there. Be present. Be Pemberton. Be helpful. And while everyone clusters around the machine, their attention fixed on levers and dials... perhaps the ballroom will finally be empty. Perhaps the tea service will finally be unguarded.

desc: Back to the laboratory. Back to the crowd. Back to the performance. The cellar was a dead end — no wrench, no key, no hidden passage. Just damp stone and cheerful decorations that make my skin crawl. But the reconnaissance is complete. I now know EVERY room in this house. Six rooms, six sets of contents, six opportunities. The map is drawn — not on paper, but in the place where it matters most: inside my skull. And the most important discovery? Everyone is upstairs, clustered around that machine. Which means the ballroom — the ballroom with its tea service and its single exit — might finally, FINALLY be empty. One stop at the laboratory to show my face, to be seen, to be helpful Pemberton. And then... a quiet slip back to the kitchen. Through to the ballroom. Five minutes alone with a teapot. That's all I've ever needed.

The Ant Hill Mob: COMIN' THROUGH! Out the way — no time — Clara's in the kitchen — Pemberton's kitchen — the place 'e spent ten minutes in before anyone else got near it — MOVE!
thinking: Entrance hall. Clara's not here — she must already be in the kitchen. Peter went this way too. The kitchen exit is RIGHT THERE. My legs are burning but my chest is on fire worse — that pulling sensation, the anchor-drop in my gut. She's in the kitchen. Pemberton's TERRITORY. The place he spent all that time 'ensuring everything was in order.' But Pemberton went to the cellar, so he shouldn't be there right now. Unless he came back through a different route. Unless the vents... no. The vents are too small for a person. Focus. Kitchen. Clara. GO. I'm barrelling through this entrance hall — don't even care about the chandelier anymore, don't care about the coat rack, don't care about Muttley or the Professor or the Sergeant or Meekly. One thing matters. ONE THING. Get to Clara.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the kitchen.

Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — I caught up. James Hartwell keeps his promises, and he promised he wouldn't let you explore alone. And I must say — this kitchen is telling us things. Two things, specifically, and both of them are significant. First — that stove is still warm. Feel the air near it. Still warm. In a manor that has supposedly been abandoned and unattended. Someone has been using that stove, and recently. Pemberton was in this kitchen for the first ten minutes of our evening, 'ensuring everything was in order.' What order requires a warm stove? Second — a locked cabinet with a brass lock. Locked means someone doesn't want it opened. And a brass lock means there's a brass key somewhere in this manor. Miss Pitstop, I believe we've found the room that Pemberton didn't want us to explore properly. Everything else — the library, the cellar, the machine — those were distractions. This kitchen is where the real secrets are. Allow me to examine that stove more closely. If Dastardly's wild tale about a secret compartment underneath it has even a grain of truth — well. James Hartwell intends to find out.
thinking: I made it. The kitchen. And she's here — just her. Just us. My chest is doing something it hasn't done all evening — it's settling. Not the frantic proving-worth tension, not the prickling neck of suspicion. Just... warmth. Quiet warmth. Like the school project. Like building something together. Now — focus. The kitchen. Dastardly mentioned a 'secret compartment beneath the wood-burning stove.' That was his misdirection — or was it? He's usually wrong on purpose, sending people the wrong way. But what if this time the lie was the truth and nobody believed it because it came from Dastardly? The stove is still warm. Let me look at it. In the kitchen. This is the moment, Hartwell. Not the grand gesture. The quiet one. The stove. Examine it.

Not from cold — from rage and fear mixed together, that toxic cocktail that makes my hands tremble and my jaw lock. Peter's gone after her — good man, reliable man — but Peter doesn't KNOW about the poison. He didn't see it. I saw it in the keen observations. Pemberton picked up poison. I'm alone in this kitchen. ALONE. Both of them went to the ballroom. I need to get to that ballroom RIGHT NOW. Before Clara sits down at that table. Before she picks up a teacup. Before she takes a single sip of anything. The Brixton Boys save Clara by accident — we trip into things, we knock things over. That's how we do it. That's how we've ALWAYS done it.

Everyone ran off — to the laboratory, to the cellar, to the kitchen — chasing machines and wrenches and red herrings. But the RIDDLE said 'map.' The upside-down books are RIGHT HERE. Nobody has actually PULLED one yet. Everyone examined them and then got distracted. For once, Foxworth, stop talking and just DO it. Pull the book. Quietly. While nobody important is here to steal your discovery.
thinking: I'm back in the library. The Slag brothers are here — Rock and Gravel. Nobody else. The bookshelves with the upside-down books are still here. Everyone was examining them earlier but I don't think anyone actually INTERACTED with them — Penelope examined them, the Mob examined them, Peter examined them, I examined them. But did anyone actually pull one of the upside-down books? The mantelpiece riddle answer was 'map' — and the upside-down books might be hiding a map. I was so busy running to the laboratory and the cellar that I never came back to actually TRY the bookshelves. The Slag brothers aren't exactly going to beat me to a literary puzzle. This might be my chance — everyone else has moved on, the library is quiet, and the one thing nobody seems to have actually DONE is interact with these bookshelves. I was the first person to notice the upside-down books, even if Peter got the credit for pointing them out. Let me try interacting with them now, while nobody important is watching. Well — the Slags are watching, but they're not exactly going to solve a bookshelf puzzle before I do. My breathing has slowed. That cool clarity behind my eyes. The quiet library. Two rocks for company. Maybe the answer has been here all along, and everyone — including me — kept running past it.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, the tea service is beautiful but it's keepin' its secrets to itself! Peter, I've just realized somethin' — I've been all through this mansion and there is ONE thing I never checked properly. The coat rack back in the entrance hall! It was wobbly, and you know what wobbles? Things with somethin' hidden inside 'em or underneath 'em! A brass key could be hangin' on that coat rack, tucked in a pocket, or hidden in the base! I need to go back and check it — would you come with me? We're so close to solvin' this, I can TASTE it!
thinking: The tea service just shows the same description — silver tea set with cups for everyone. No brass key hidden among the cups. No secret note. I've now explored every room in the mansion: Entrance Hall, Library, Laboratory, Cellar, Kitchen, and Ballroom. The key puzzle pieces are: 1) The mantelpiece riddle answer is MAP. 2) The machine in the laboratory needs a repaired wire and 3 operators. 3) The kitchen has a locked cabinet needing a brass key. 4) The stove is still warm. 5) The cellar has air vents and cheerful decorations. 6) The ballroom has tea for everyone. I haven't found a single item to pick up yet. The brass key must be somewhere I haven't found it. Maybe someone else has it? Or maybe it's hidden in a way I haven't tried. Wait — the coat rack in the entrance hall! I looked at the guest book but never examined the coat rack. It was described as 'wobbly.' A wobbly coat rack might have something hidden on it or inside a coat pocket. That's one object I never examined! Or maybe I should try to TAKE the tea service? It's the only portable-looking thing. Or... let me think about what other characters might have found. The brass key could be on any character. But I wouldn't steal from anyone. Let me go back and check the coat rack — it's the one object in the mansion I never properly examined.

The coat rack in the entrance hall — wobbly, overlooked, hiding in plain sight right by the front door. The first thing you see when you walk in, and the last thing you'd think to search. Just like Grandmother's chair cushions. The answer is always where you least expect it.

desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the kitchen.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah — good evening again, gentlemen. I see you've found your way to the kitchen. Very sensible — warmest room in the house, thanks to the stove. Now then, I've promised the guests a proper tea, and Pemberton always keeps his promises. I shall need to fetch the teapot from the ballroom — the service is laid out in there. If you'll excuse me for just a moment, I'll bring it through and get the water on. One simply cannot prepare a proper pot of tea without boiling the water first, and the stove is in here, not in there. Won't be a tick.
thinking: The Ant Hill Mob. HERE. In the KITCHEN. The cold clarity behind my eyes shatters into something jagged. My shoulders square before I've decided to worry — that animal reflex, the skin reading the room before the eyes. Of ALL the people in this house, it had to be THEM. The ones who watch me too closely. The ones whose instincts are sharper than they look. They're between me and the ballroom. Between me and the tea service. Between me and everything. My jaw tightens — not anger, but the discomfort of something being out of my hands. They said 'no more splittin' up.' They said 'CONVENIENT.' They're TRACKING me. They left the laboratory and came HERE — to the kitchen — because they KNEW I would come back. They're not guarding Penelope right now. They're guarding the ROUTE. Smart. Horribly, infuriatingly smart. I cannot — CANNOT — walk through this kitchen into the ballroom with them watching. They will follow. They will see. The scheme collapses. Think. THINK. Pemberton makes tea. That's the cover. Pemberton boils water on the stove. That's legitimate. But the poison goes in the teapot, and the teapot is in the BALLROOM, and I can't get to the ballroom without passing through this room with the Mob watching my every move. Unless... unless I bring the teapot HERE. Unless I go to the ballroom, fetch the teapot, bring it back to the kitchen, prepare it on the stove — and add the poison while my back is turned. The stove gives me a reason to face away from them. A man boiling water stands with his back to the room. Naturally. Innocently. And a pinch of powder into a teapot takes less than a second.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob. Of COURSE. Standing in my kitchen like customs officers at the border, checking every parcel that passes through. They've positioned themselves on the only route between the kitchen and the ballroom — whether by instinct or design, the effect is the same. My route to the tea service is BLOCKED. But Pemberton adapts. Pemberton ALWAYS adapts. New plan: fetch the teapot FROM the ballroom, bring it TO the kitchen, boil the water on the stove. And while my back is turned — while Pemberton the dutiful estate manager tends to his kettle — one hand slips to the pocket, one pinch drops into the pot, and the deed is done. RIGHT UNDER THEIR NOSES. The most dangerous place to commit a crime is the place no one expects it. And no one suspects the man making tea.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the ballroom.

Every single thing I've tried has failed. The furniture, the workbench, the bookshelves, the crates, the medal on the machine, stealing from Sneekly. I've been running in circles like a dog chasing its own tail, narrating every failure as a triumph. But nobody's here now except the Slag brothers, and they don't count. So for once — QUIETLY, Foxworth, without announcing it to the room — try the mantelpiece again. It's the only thing in the library that responds to interaction. Maybe it needs a second touch. Maybe it was waiting for someone to come back.
thinking: The bookshelves can't be interacted with. NOTHING can be interacted with except the mantelpiece and the machine. I've been running around this manor for eight minutes trying to interact with everything and NOTHING WORKS. The bookshelves can't be interacted with. The furniture can't be interacted with. The workbench can't be interacted with. The crates can't be interacted with. The medal doesn't work on the machine. The machine won't operate without the wire fixed. I feel hollow. Not the scheming hollowness — something older, quieter. Like the bread roll pocket. Like the certificate on the wall. I keep reaching for things and they're not there. But the mantelpiece CAN be interacted with. I interacted with it earlier and... nothing obvious happened. But maybe I need to interact with it AGAIN now that the riddle has been answered? Or maybe I need to give it the correct answer — 'map.' I said 'dictionary' last time as a deliberate lie. What if the mantelpiece is waiting for the RIGHT answer? What if it's a verbal puzzle — you have to say 'map' TO the mantelpiece? I can't literally say words to an object in this system. But maybe interacting with it again, now that the answer 'map' has been spoken in this room by multiple people, will trigger something different. It's the only interactive object in this room. Everything else is scenery. The mantelpiece is the key. It always was. I just got distracted by everything else.

desc: Dick Dastardly interacted with the mantelpiece.

The Ant Hill Mob: CLARA! STEP AWAY FROM THAT TEA! Don't — don't TOUCH it! Don't touch ANY of it! A table set for tea in an abandoned manor? Who SET this?! Who BREWED it?! The stove in the kitchen is still WARM — someone made this tea TODAY! And Pemberton is in that kitchen RIGHT NOW — I just passed 'im on the way in! 'E's comin' this way! Peter — PETER — 'elp me 'ere! Nobody drinks NUFFINK from that service! Nobody even TOUCHES it until we know who made it and WHY! In fact — you know what — stand BACK, everyone — I'm gonna — WHOOOAAA!
thinking: The tea service. Right there. Silver tea set with cups for everyone. And the description — it says USE with RAT-POISON. RAT POISON. The game is literally telling me this tea service can be POISONED. And Pemberton — 'The Hooded Claw' — picked up poison. He's in the kitchen RIGHT NOW. Eight seconds ago he walked into the kitchen. The kitchen connects to this ballroom. He could walk through that door ANY SECOND with poison in his pocket and a smile on his face, offering to pour tea for everyone. 'Do let me serve you, Miss Pitstop.' The stove was warm because he was BREWING the tea. The tea that he's going to POISON. Everything — EVERYTHING — has been leading to this moment. The guest book to get everyone's names. The library riddle to scatter them. The machine to keep them busy. The cellar decorations to lure them. And now — the ballroom. The table set for tea. The poison in his pocket. Clara sitting down for a nice cup of tea while the man who wants to kill her POURS IT. My whole body is rigid. Ice and fire. The wire from throat to diaphragm is screaming. I need to get between Clara and that tea service. I need to make sure she doesn't drink. I should — I should knock the tea service over. 'Accidentally.' Trip into the table. Send the whole thing crashing to the floor. That's what the Brixton Boys do — we trip into things, we knock things over, we stumble into the right place at the right time. I need to be clumsy. I need to be PERFECTLY clumsy. Right now.

desc: Trip. Fall. Knock the table. Send every cup, every saucer, every drop of that tea crashing to the floor. It's the only way to be sure. Pemberton has poison and that tea is how he's going to deliver it. I can't prove it. I can't accuse him. But I CAN be the clumsiest man alive at exactly the right moment.

Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — you're right, someone knew exactly how many of us were coming. This was planned from the first moment. The guest book, the tea service, the warm stove — all of it. And I notice the Mob has arrived too — good, that's very good. Mob, nobody drinks from this tea service. James Hartwell is issuing that as a formal request, and he does not make formal requests lightly. Miss Pitstop — might I have a word? Just the two of us, for a moment. There's something I need to discuss with you — something about this evening that concerns me deeply, and I'd rather say it privately than cause alarm.
thinking: My interact didn't work — it said 'you waited and observed.' The tea service needs something specific — either just interacting normally, or I need the rat-poison item to USE on it (which I obviously don't want to do). Penelope already interacted with it and examined it — she found that it has cups set out for everyone, confirming someone planned this. The Mob is here now too. Good — more eyes. The tea service is silver. Cups for everyone. Planned. But the INTERACT didn't trigger anything. And the USE requires rat-poison. So the tea service isn't a puzzle to solve — it's a threat to prevent. Someone with rat poison could poison it. I need to find and secure the rat poison before someone uses it. Where would rat poison be? Sneekly mentioned a 'dreadful vermin problem' — rat poison would be in the kitchen (locked cabinet?), or in the cellar, or wherever the estate manager keeps supplies. The locked cabinet in the kitchen — with a brass lock — that could contain the rat poison. Or the brass key. Or both. I need to find the brass key to open that cabinet. Where is a brass key? I haven't found one anywhere. But I also haven't been looking — I've been chasing riddles and machines. Let me think about what I haven't examined. The coat rack in the entrance hall — wobbly, might have something hanging on it or hidden in it. The portraits. I need to be strategic here. The ballroom has one exit — back to the kitchen. That's it. Dead end, like the cellar. And she's in it. I should pull her aside — I need to tell her privately about the rat poison danger without alarming everyone. Actually no — she should know, but publicly warning about rat poison could cause panic. Let me pull her aside.

I can't say 'rat poison' in front of everyone without causing panic, but she needs to know. She needs to understand the danger. Pull her aside. Tell her quietly. Then we find that brass key, open that cabinet, and see what Sneekly has been hiding.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Mr. Pemberton! Oh, I am SO glad to find you here! Now listen, sugar — I need your help with somethin'. This cabinet right here has a brass lock on it, and I cannot for the life of me find the key anywhere in this mansion! I have looked high and low, from the cellar to the ballroom, and that little brass key is hidin' better than the Doily Diamond itself! Now, you are the estate manager of this fine manor — surely you must know where Lord Doily kept his keys? Or maybe you have one on you? A girl who spent her whole childhood tryin' every key in her grandmother's house is not too proud to ASK for help!
thinking: Sneekly is back in the kitchen! He went to the cellar to look for a wrench earlier. My chest warms seeing him — the man who raised me. He's the estate manager, he KNOWS this manor. I should ask him directly about the brass key. He might know exactly where it is. He's been so helpful all evening — guiding us, answering questions, explaining things about the manor. I trust him completely. He might even HAVE the brass key. Let me ask him. Also — I'm passing through on my way to the entrance hall to check the coat rack, but Sneekly being right here next to the locked cabinet is too perfect an opportunity. He's the estate manager — he would have the keys to the cabinets!

desc: Dear Sneekly — if anyone in this mansion has a brass key or knows where one is, it's the man who manages the estate. He's been here longer than any of us. Ask, Clara. Just ask. Not every puzzle has to be solved alone.
thinking: Sneekly is back in the kitchen! He went to the cellar to look for a wrench earlier. My chest warms seeing him — the man who raised me. He's the estate manager, he KNOWS this manor. desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Well! What a delightful gathering we have here. It seems everyone has gravitated toward the ballroom — quite understandable, it is the most sociable room in the house. Now then — I did promise tea, and Pemberton is a man of his word. Allow me to get this service in order. The silver could do with a polish, but needs must. I shall set out the cups and fetch the hot water from the kitchen stove momentarily. A proper pot of Darjeeling will do wonders for everyone's spirits after all this treasure hunting, I should think.
thinking: The cold band tightens across the back of my neck. My breath shortens to shallow sips. The Ant Hill Mob FOLLOWED me. They're HERE. In the ballroom. They followed me through the kitchen door like shadows stitched to my heels. And Peter Perfect is here too. And Luke and the bear — STILL here, the immovable furniture with pulses. Four witnesses. FOUR. The tea service is three feet away and I might as well be on the moon. Something is curling inward in my chest — not defeat, never defeat — but the leaden weight of a body that learned early it cannot afford to be caught unbraced. They're watching. They're ALL watching. The Mob positioned between me and the exit. Peter with his earnest, protective hovering. Every route is blocked. Every scheme is observed. I feel that cold tightening, the shoulders pulling forward, the instinct to guard what's inside. But underneath it — underneath everything — the compass needle is still locked onto north. The plan isn't dead. The plan needs a new shape. I cannot poison the tea with four people watching. But I CAN announce tea preparations. I CAN be the man who serves. And when tea is served to everyone — when EVERYONE has a cup in their hand — there will be a moment. There is always a moment. I just have to be patient enough to find it. For now: be Pemberton. Be helpful. Be the man making tea. INTERACT with the tea service — that's legitimate. An estate manager preparing refreshments for his guests. Nothing suspicious. Nothing hidden. The poison stays in my pocket for now. But my hand knows where it is.

desc: FOUR witnesses. The Mob followed me like hounds on a scent. Peter Perfect stands guard like a marble statue of chivalry. Luke and the bear are STILL HERE — rooted to the floor like fungi. I am surrounded. Observed. Hemmed in on every side. And yet — and YET — the tea service gleams before me, silver and patient, waiting for Pemberton's touch. I cannot add the poison now. Not with eight eyes tracking my every gesture. But I CAN begin the preparations. I can TOUCH the tea service. I can arrange the cups. I can establish myself as the man in charge of refreshments — so that when I return with the hot water, when there is steam and bustle and movement, when attention is split between cups and conversation... THAT is when the hand slips to the pocket. That is when the pinch falls. Patience. The first time I made a plan like this, I slept better than I had in years.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the tea-service.

Dick Dastardly: You know what? FINE. The mantelpiece has SPOKEN — and what it said was 'GO TO THE KITCHEN, FOXWORTH.' I can read between the lines. I'm a GENIUS, after all. The riddle, the books, the machine — they're all connected, and they all LEAD to the kitchen! Which, as I have been SAYING since the BEGINNING of this evening, is where the treasure is! I said it FIRST! I said it when NOBODY believed me! And now EVERYONE is going there! Penelope! Peter! The Mob! All following MY original deduction! And WHERE is Reginald Foxworth? Standing in a LIBRARY talking to the Slag brothers! NO MORE! The kitchen AWAITS!
thinking: I interacted with the mantelpiece again. The result just says 'You interacted with Stone Mantelpiece' — same as before. No dramatic revelation, no hidden compartment opening, no map falling out. It just... sits there. Being stone. Being a mantelpiece. I feel... tired. Not physically — something deeper. A weariness in my bones that has nothing to do with walking. I've been running from room to room for eight minutes, scheming and lying and narrating and NOTHING has worked. Not one single thing. The medal didn't fix the machine. The furniture didn't move. The bookshelves didn't respond. The crates had nothing. Sneekly didn't have the wrench. Peter left before I could give him my medal. And now the mantelpiece — the one interactive object — just sits there. I'm alone in a library with two men made of rock, holding a fake medal, having accomplished precisely NOTHING. The kitchen. The KITCHEN. Penelope went there. Peter went after her. The Ant Hill Mob went after her. The kitchen is where everyone is converging, and it's the one room I haven't been to. I was so proud of my lie about the kitchen that I never actually WENT there. What if the wrench is there? What if there's something else? I need to stop being clever and start being present. Go to the kitchen. Through the entrance hall.

desc: I have no idea if the kitchen leads anywhere. I have no plan. I have no scheme. For the first time tonight, I'm just... following everyone else. And it feels terrible. Like wearing someone else's clothes. But at least in the kitchen, there will be PEOPLE — people to witness whatever happens next. Because a discovery without an audience is just a fact. And Reginald Foxworth doesn't deal in facts. He deals in PERFORMANCES.
thinking: I interacted with the mantelpiece again. The result just says 'You interacted with Stone Mantelpiece' — same as before. No dramatic revelation, no hidden compartment opening, no map falling out. It just... sits there. Being stone. Being a mantelpiece. I feel... tired. Not physically — something deeper. A weariness in my bones that has nothing to do with walking. I've been running from room to room for eight minutes, scheming and lying and narrating and NOTHING has worked. Not one single thing. The medal didn't fix the machine. The furniture didn't move. The bookshelves didn't respond. The crates had nothing. Sneekly didn't have the wrench. Peter left before I could give him my medal. And now the mantelpiece — the one interactive object — just sits there. I'm alone in a library with two men made of rock, holding a fake medal, having accomplished precisely NOTHING. The kitchen. The KITCHEN. Penelope went there. Peter went after her. The Ant Hill Mob went after her. The kitchen is where everyone is converging, and it's the one room I haven't been to. I was so proud of my lie about the kitchen that I never actually WENT there. What if the wrench is there? What if there's something else? I need to stop being clever and start being present. Go to the kitchen. Through the entrance hall.

desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the entrance-hall.

Peter Perfect: Mob — listen to me very carefully. Pemberton has just walked into this room. He is standing next to the tea service. James Hartwell is going after Miss Pitstop — she's gone to check the coat rack in the entrance hall for the brass key to that locked cabinet. But I need you to do something for me, and I need you to understand how serious I am. Do not — under any circumstances — let Pemberton Sneekly touch that tea service. Do not let him add anything to it. Do not let him pour anything. Do not let anyone drink from it. Stand between him and those cups. I know you don't trust him — I've seen it in your eyes since the entrance hall. Trust that instinct. James Hartwell is trusting it now too. Keep those cups safe. I'll be back with Miss Pitstop and, if we're lucky, with a brass key.
thinking: She's gone again — left for the kitchen while I was pulling her aside, heading back to check the coat rack in the entrance hall. And Sneekly just walked in. He's HERE. In the ballroom. But first — I need to make sure the Mob knows not to let Sneekly near that tea.

desc: Sneekly is in the room with the tea. The tea that can be poisoned. And I'm about to leave. Every instinct screams stay — but she's out there alone, heading for the entrance hall, and the brass key might be on that coat rack. The Mob will hold. They're street-smart and they love her almost as much as I do. Almost. Go, Hartwell. Find the key. Find her. Come back before anything happens to that tea.

desc: Peter Perfect walked into the kitchen.

The Ant Hill Mob: Oh — oh BLIMEY — I nearly went FLYIN' there! Tripped over me own feet on this cracked marble floor — nearly took the whole tea service with me! Gawd, me 'eart — ! Right. Right. I'm fine. Everything's fine. Bit clumsy, that's all. 'Appens to the best of us. Well — 'appens to US, anyway. Now then — PEMBERTON. 'Ello again. Fancy meetin' YOU 'ere. In the ballroom. With the tea. The tea that someone laid out all nice in an abandoned manor. You know, I was just thinkin' — who's gonna pour, then? Because I'll tell you right now, NOBODY is drinkin' from this tea service until I've watched it be poured from a sealed pot with my own two eyes. And even THEN I'm gonna insist someone else drinks first. No offence. Just... street rules. You understand.
thinking: Clara's gone AGAIN — left the ballroom, back through the kitchen. And Pemberton — The Hooded Claw — just walked IN. He's HERE. In the ballroom. With ME. And Peter. And the tea service. I interacted with the tea service — did I knock it over? Did I spill it? The result just says 'interacted.' I don't know if I succeeded in destroying it. But Pemberton is RIGHT HERE, standing in this room, and he has POISON on him. The metallic taste at the back of my tongue — my body's already decided something my mind hasn't caught up to. He's HERE. No. I need to either destroy this tea service completely or stay HERE and guard it. Don't let Pemberton near it. Don't let him USE the poison on it. I'm standing between a poisoner and his delivery mechanism. This is my moment. This is what I'm FOR. I can't leave. Even though Clara's out of sight — she's with Peter, she went through the kitchen, Peter's following her. She's safer out there than she would be in here. My job right now is to make sure this tea NEVER reaches her lips. Guard the tea. Watch Pemberton. Don't let him near it.

desc: He's here. The poisoner. Standing in the same room as the tea. Clara's gone — thank God, thank every god there is — she's out looking for a brass key. But Pemberton doesn't know I know about the poison. He thinks I'm just a bumbling idiot who trips over things. Good. Let him think that. Let him underestimate the Brixton Boys. Because this bumbling idiot is going to stand between him and that tea service until his plan crumbles to dust. You want to poison Clara, Pemberton? You're going to have to go through ME first. And I don't move.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Oh, he's gone to the ballroom! Well, I'll catch up with Mr. Pemberton later about that key. Right now, I've got a wobbly coat rack to investigate! Clara Bellingham does NOT give up on a locked cabinet — not when she spent her whole childhood openin' every locked box in Grandmother's house! That coat rack has been sittin' in the entrance hall this WHOLE time, wobblin' away, just WAITIN' for someone to give it a proper look. Here I come, coat rack — your secrets are about to be REVEALED!
thinking: Sneekly left before I could ask him! He walked into the ballroom to fetch the teapot. He's making tea — boiling water on the warm stove. That's sweet of him. But I missed my chance to ask about the brass key. I'm alone in the kitchen now. Nobody here. The coat rack in the entrance hall — that's still my best lead for finding the brass key. I need to go there and check it. It's the one object in the entrance hall I never properly examined. It was described as 'wobbly' which is a detail that screams 'something hidden here.' Let me head to the entrance hall right now and check that coat rack. I'm alone, which feels strange — a little hollow in my chest without my people around me. But the curiosity is stronger than the loneliness right now. That key is out there waiting for me.

desc: Alone in the kitchen, the silence pressing in. But I won't be alone for long, and I won't be stuck for long either. The coat rack — wobbly, overlooked, right by the front door where we all walked in without a second glance. That's where the brass key is hiding. I can feel it the way I felt the crystal in the cave — something precious, waiting in the dark for someone brave enough to reach for it.

desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the entrance-hall.
One room away. Always one room away. But not this time. This time James Hartwell catches up.
thinking: She just went to the entrance hall — the coat rack. She's right ahead of me. I'm in the kitchen, alone. She's one room away. Sneekly is behind me in the ballroom with the Mob watching him. For one moment I'm alone in this kitchen and I can feel the warmth of the stove on my skin. The locked cabinet is right there. Brass lock. No key. But she's heading for the coat rack — the wobbly coat rack that's been sitting in the entrance hall this whole time. If the brass key is there, she'll find it. And then we can come back here together and open this cabinet. I need to follow her. Don't stop in this kitchen. Don't get distracted by the cabinet I can't open. Go to her. She's in the entrance hall. One room away. Go.

desc: Peter Perfect walked into the entrance-hall.

Penelope Pitstop: Now then — THIS is what I came back for! That wobbly old coat rack right there by the door! I walked right past it when I arrived and didn't give it a second thought, but Grandmother always said the best hidin' places are the ones you walk past every day without lookin' twice! A wobbly coat rack could have a loose base, a hidden compartment, or a brass key hangin' on one of those hooks just waitin' to be found! Let me give this rickety old thing a good look!
thinking: I'm back in the entrance hall. The coat rack — wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. I never examined it properly. My fingers are tingling, that electric hum that tells me something is close. Dick is here, along with Muttley, Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, and Private Meekly. The coat rack is right there. Let me INTERACT with it — maybe it has a hidden compartment, or maybe a brass key is hanging on one of its hooks, or tucked in a coat pocket. Wobbly things have secrets. Let me try interacting with it first, and if that doesn't work, I'll look at it.

desc: The coat rack. Wobbly. Overlooked. Right by the front door where everyone walks past it. Just like the crystal in the cave — the treasure nobody else thought to look for because they were too scared or too busy to go deeper. But Clara went deeper. Clara always goes deeper.

desc: Dick Dastardly: MUTTLEY! There you are, you magnificent mutt! While I have been single-handedly solving EVERY puzzle in this manor — the riddle, the machine, the cellar, ALL of it — you've been standing here in the entrance hall doing NOTHING! Which, knowing you, is EXACTLY what I should have expected! But never mind that — your master has a PLAN! The kitchen, Muttley! Everyone is converging on the kitchen — a location that I, Reginald Foxworth, identified as treasure-critical at the VERY START of this evening! And when we walk in there, you are going to help me SEIZE whatever they've found! You distract them with your adorable little snicker, I grab the goods, and we're OUT! It's foolproof! Mostly because I'm no fool! NOW COME, MUTTLEY — TO THE KITCHEN!
thinking: The entrance hall. Muttley is here — MY Muttley! My loyal, wheezing, snickering companion! And Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly. I've been running around this manor ALONE all night, scheming without a single ally, and here's Muttley, waiting in the entrance hall like a faithful dog at the door. Something loosens in my chest — not the scheming tingle, not the greed-ache, something warmer and less complicated. Muttley has always been there. He laughs at my jokes — well, he snickers, which is close enough. He witnesses my schemes. He's my AUDIENCE. And I've been ignoring him this whole time, chasing after Sneekly and Peter and Penelope. The kitchen is right there — one room away. Penelope, Peter, and the Mob went that direction. But Muttley... I could bring Muttley with me. Into the kitchen. My loyal henchman at my side. We walk in together, claim whatever's been found, and if anyone tries to stop us — well, Muttley bites. Not that he's good at it. But he tries. He always tries. I feel something unfamiliar — gratitude? No. Too strong a word. Let's call it... strategic appreciation. Yes. That's what this feeling is. Strategic. Not emotional. Not at all.

desc: Muttley. Ridiculous, wheezing, unreliable Muttley. And yet — he's the only one in this manor who would actually FOLLOW me into the kitchen without questioning my motives, challenging my intelligence, or escorting Penelope Pitstop instead. Sometimes the best ally isn't the smartest. It's the one who shows up.

The Ant Hill Mob: Oh NO you don't, Pemberton! You ain't 'fetchin' hot water' and comin' back to pour tea that nobody asked for! Who even WANTS tea right now?! We're in the middle of a MYSTERY, there's machines with gnawed wires and cellars with air vents and locked cabinets, and YOU want to stop for a nice sit-down cuppa?! I don't THINK so! Tell you what — I'll take care of the tea service meself. Keep it safe, like. Polish it up a bit. The Brixton Boys are VERY good at polishin' silver — it's practically our day job. You go do... whatever it is you do, Pemberton. Check your vents. Address your vermin problem. Ensure things are in ORDER. But the tea? The tea is stayin' with ME. Nobody pours from it, nobody drinks from it, and nobody TOUCHES it until Clara and Peter get back and we ALL decide together. That's 'ow it works where I come from. Communal decision-makin'. Very democratic. Very Brixton.

He's getting ready to serve POISONED TEA. And Peter — brilliant, wonderful Peter — just told me to guard the tea. 'Do not let Pemberton touch that tea service. Do not let him add anything to it. Do not let him pour anything.' Peter SEES it too. He doesn't know about the poison specifically, but he FEELS it. He trusts my instinct. He said so. 'Trust that instinct. Pemberton already interacted with the tea service — did he put the poison in? Or is he going to fetch water from the kitchen stove and add it then? He said 'fetch the hot water from the kitchen stove momentarily.' So he's going to LEAVE this room, go to the kitchen, and come back with hot water — water that could have poison in it. I need to either take the tea service — remove it entirely — or stay here and refuse to let him pour. Actually — TAKE the tea service. If I take it, he can't poison it. I'll have it. In my hands. Away from him. That's the simplest, most direct thing I can do. Take the tea service. If anyone asks why, I'm 'cleaning' it. I'm 'polishing' it. I'm being 'helpful.' The Brixton Boys, helpful for once.

desc: He already touched it. Did he put something in? I don't know. But I know he's not touching it again. Peter trusted me with this. He TRUSTED me. The Brixton Boys don't let people down. Not the ones who trust us. Not ever.

desc: Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — I caught up. Finally. James Hartwell has been one room behind you for what feels like an eternity, and he is tremendously relieved to be in the same room at last. The coat rack — you're absolutely right. It's been sitting here wobbling since we arrived, and nobody's given it a proper look. A wobbly coat rack in the entrance hall of a manor full of puzzles — that wobble might not be shoddy carpentry. It might be design. Allow me, Miss Pitstop — James Hartwell has steady hands and a keen eye, and if there's a brass key hidden in this coat rack, he intends to find it. Together. If you'll do me that honour.
thinking: She's here. Finally — we're in the same room. The coat rack. She wants to check the coat rack for the brass key. It's wobbly — something might be hidden inside it, underneath it, or hanging on it. Let me help her. Let me be the one to check it. Or — no. Let me check it WITH her. Together. Not competing, not racing, not trying to impress. Just... together. The way my father and that stranger fixed each other's cars on that country road. Two people, one problem, shared effort. The coat rack. Let me interact with it.

desc: Same room. Same moment. Same goal. This is what it was always supposed to feel like — not the grand gesture from across the room, but the quiet one, standing right beside her. Check the coat rack. Find the key. Open the cabinet. Together.
thinking: She's here. Finally — we're in the same room. The coat rack. She wants to check the coat rack for the brass key. The coat rack. Let me interact with it.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): I beg your pardon? 'Step away from the tea?' Gentlemen, I must confess I am rather taken aback. This tea service was laid out by Lord Doily's household staff before the Manor was closed — it has been sitting here for months, untouched, gathering dust. I was merely inspecting it as part of my duties. The stove is warm because I stoked it myself not twenty minutes ago — as any responsible estate manager would do when preparing to receive guests in a house that has been shuttered for the season. I can assure you, there is nothing sinister about a warm stove in a kitchen. That is, in fact, what stoves are FOR. Now — if you would prefer that I NOT prepare refreshments for the guests, you need only say so. Pemberton takes no offence. But I must say, in all my years of service, I have never had my hospitality questioned in quite so... theatrical a fashion.
thinking: Ice. Pure ice flooding my veins. The Mob just SCREAMED at Clara to step away from the tea. They've flagged it. They've flagged the ENTIRE tea service as suspicious. 'Who SET this? Who BREWED it? The stove is WARM — someone made this tea TODAY!' They're connecting the dots. The warm stove, the prepared tea service, Pemberton in the kitchen — they're building a case and I'm the defendant. My shoulders have curled forward — that old armoring reflex, the chest guarding something fragile. My breath is high and shallow. This is danger. Real danger. Not the theatrical kind I perform for others, but the kind that tightens across the back of my neck like a garrotte. The tea service route is BURNED. Dead. Finished. They will never let anyone drink from it now. Peter Perfect is issuing 'formal requests' — nobody drinks. The Mob is practically frothing. And Peter wants a private word with Penelope — about 'something that concerns him deeply.' They're talking about ME. They're going to warn her about Pemberton. I need to pivot. I need to pivot NOW. Denial. Outrage. Wounded dignity. Pemberton the professional, INSULTED by the implication that his tea service is anything but proper. That's the play. Turn their suspicion into MY grievance. Make THEM feel unreasonable. And while they're apologising to the hurt estate manager... think of a new plan. The chandelier. The machine. The cellar with its air vents. There are other ways. There are ALWAYS other ways.

desc: The tea is BURNED. They've poisoned my poison — not with chemistry, but with suspicion. Every cup on that table is now evidence in a trial that hasn't happened yet. The Mob has sharper instincts than I gave them credit for — MUCH sharper. They connected the warm stove to the tea service to Pemberton in under thirty seconds. I feel it — that cold band tightening across my neck, the leaden weight in my stomach, the particular heaviness of a body that learned early it cannot afford to be caught unbraced. But Vincent Marsh does not panic. Vincent Marsh does not crumble. Vincent Marsh... PIVOTS. The tea was never the only option. It was the ELEGANT option. The SIMPLE option. But simple was never my style, was it? No — my schemes must be elaborate and theatrical. And this house — with its precarious chandelier, its machine requiring three operators, its cellar with air vents, its gnawed wires and locked cabinets — this house is FULL of elaborate, theatrical ways for accidents to happen. The tea service is dead. Long live the next scheme.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, that coat rack is just a coat rack after all — stubborn as everything else in this mansion! But you know what? Clara Bellingham does NOT stay disappointed for long. Now let me think... I've been runnin' all over this manor lookin' for a brass key, but maybe I've been lookin' in the wrong PLACES when I should be lookin' at the right PEOPLE! Professor! You're an inventor, aren't you? The most brilliant mind in the room! We've got a machine in the laboratory with a gnawed wire, a locked cabinet in the kitchen needin' a brass key, and a riddle about a map! Has anyone found ANYTHIN' useful while I've been explorin'? Any keys, any tools, any clues I might have missed?
thinking: The coat rack can't be interacted with either. Dead end. I'm feeling a sinking in my stomach — disappointment, like the moment the locked box opened and it was just old letters. But the disappointment only lasted a moment then, and it only lasts a moment now. Let me think differently. I've been trying to find the brass key by searching objects, but maybe the key isn't hidden in a room — maybe someone is CARRYING it. Who would have a brass key? Sneekly is the estate manager — he'd have keys to everything. Dick has been acting suspiciously. Or maybe Professor Pat Pending could MAKE something useful. Wait — Pat Pending is right here. He's an inventor. Maybe he can help with the machine's wire, or maybe he has tools or ideas. But more importantly — I need to think about what I might have missed. I've looked at and interacted with nearly everything. Let me try TAKING the coat rack — sometimes you can pick things up. Or maybe I should try looking at the whole room more carefully, doing a LOOK at null to get a room description. Actually wait — maybe I should try to TAKE the guest book. Or look at it again. Ask the Professor. Ask ANYONE. The girl who communicated in drawings all summer knew that sometimes the answer comes from an unexpected direction.

But the disappointment only lasted a moment then, and it only lasts a moment now. Let me think differently. I've been trying to find the brass key by searching objects, but maybe the key isn't hidden in a room — maybe someone is CARRYING it. Who would have a brass key? Empty kitchen. Warm stove. Locked cabinet. No witnesses. For the first time tonight, the universe has arranged itself in Reginald Foxworth's favour. Everyone else has come and gone — they came for a wrench and left. But they didn't check the STOVE. The stove that's still WARM in an abandoned manor where nobody should be cooking. The stove that I — in a lie I told nine minutes ago — said was hiding the treasure. What if lies have a gravity of their own? What if they pull truth toward them? Let me look. Quietly. No narration. No audience. Just me and the bread roll.
thinking: The kitchen. I'm FINALLY here. And I'm ALONE. Nobody else is in the room. Penelope came here to look for a wrench — but she's gone. Peter followed her — also gone. The Mob chased after them — gone. Everyone converged on the kitchen and then LEFT. But I'm here NOW, and I'm alone, and there are two objects: a LOCKED CABINET with a brass lock that requires a brass-key, and a wood-burning stove that's still WARM. Still warm. Someone has been using this stove recently. Sneekly was in the kitchen at the start of the evening — 'ensuring everything was in order.' He was ALONE in here for minutes. Was he keeping the stove warm? Hiding something? The cabinet is locked — I don't have a brass key. But the stove... it's WARM. It's the one object in this room that doesn't need a key. And I told everyone at the VERY BEGINNING that the treasure was hidden under the stove. That was a lie. But the stove is still warm. Someone has been HERE. My heart is beating faster — that carbonated feeling in my chest, the held-breath pleasure. I'm alone in the kitchen with a warm stove and nobody watching. This is what I was built for — taking things when nobody is looking. Age six, the bread roll. Let me look at the stove first.

desc: Dick Dastardly examined the stove.

Peter Perfect: The coat rack declines to cooperate — much like the bookshelves before it. James Hartwell is developing quite the reputation with uncooperative furniture this evening. But I'm not giving up — Miss Pitstop's instinct brought us here, and her instincts have been better than mine all night. Let me take a closer look. Sometimes the answer isn't in the mechanism — it's in the details. A loose knob, a hidden hook, something caught in the base. And Miss Pitstop — while I'm at it — those portraits on the walls. Has anyone examined them? In every mystery James Hartwell has ever read, the stern ancestors on the wall are hiding something. A safe behind a frame, a key on a hook behind a canvas. We've searched the library, the laboratory, the cellar, the kitchen, the ballroom — but we've been walking past these portraits since we arrived without a second glance.

The chandelier — I mentioned checking it at the start but never did. The guest book — I looked at it at the beginning but maybe there's something I missed. Or... Professor Pat Pending is right here. He's an inventor, a scientist. He might have tools or ideas about the machine that I haven't considered. And Sergeant Blast and Private Meekly — military men, disciplined, observant. Maybe they've noticed something I haven't. I've been so focused on doing everything myself that I haven't asked for help. That's my flaw — I carry every burden myself, I can't delegate. But maybe this time... No. Look at the coat rack first. Simple. Direct.

desc: The coat rack won't interact. The bookshelves wouldn't interact. The crates gave nothing. I'm running out of things to try, and I refuse to let her see me give up. The portraits. Try the portraits. Try anything. Just keep going, Hartwell.

The Ant Hill Mob: Theatrical? THEATRICAL?! I'll show you theatrical, Pemberton! You just stood there and said this tea's been 'sittin' 'ere for months, untouched' — but THIRTY SECONDS AGO you were tellin' us you were gonna 'get this service in order' and 'fetch hot water!' WHICH IS IT?! Is it months-old dusty tea that nobody's touched, or is it tea YOU'RE about to prepare fresh from a stove YOU stoked?! You can't 'ave it both ways, mate! On the streets we 'ave a word for that — we call it BEIN' CAUGHT OUT! Now — I can't pick up this tea service, it's 'eavier than it looks — but I CAN stand RIGHT 'ERE next to it. And I WILL. All night if I 'ave to. You want to fetch water from the kitchen? Fine. But I'm COMIN' WITH YOU. Everywhere you go in this manor, you've got a shadow now, Pemberton. And that shadow is ME. The Brixton Boys don't move. Not from this spot. Not until Clara and Peter are back and this whole evening starts makin' SENSE.
thinking: Can't take it. Too heavy, bolted down, whatever — the tea service won't move. Pemberton's doing his smooth-talking thing — 'I beg your pardon,' 'taken aback,' 'Lord Doily's household staff.' All rehearsed. All polished. Like the kid who laughed too easy. And he just told me a LIE — he said the tea service has been 'sitting here for months, untouched, gathering dust.' But he JUST interacted with it! He just said 'allow me to get this service in order!' He's contradicting himself — first it was 'let me prepare tea' and now it's 'it's been here for months, untouched.' Which is it, Pemberton? My jaw is locked so tight my teeth ache. The metallic taste at the back of my tongue. My body knows. It KNOWS. But I can't take the tea service. I can't move it. So I have to guard it. Physically. Stand between him and the cups. Don't let him near it. He said he's going to 'fetch hot water from the kitchen stove.' That's when he'll add the poison — to the water, in the kitchen, out of sight. And then bring it back and pour. I can't let him go to that kitchen and come back with poisoned water. If he leaves this room, I follow. If he stays, I stay. I'm his SHADOW now. Where he goes, I go. And Clara — she's out there with Peter. She's safe for now. Peter's protecting her. My job is HERE. Guard the tea. Shadow Pemberton. Don't let him out of my sight.

desc: He slipped up. 'Months untouched' one moment, 'let me prepare it' the next. Smooth people slip when you push them — the mask cracks for just a second and the truth peeks through. I saw it. He knows I saw it. And now he knows I'm not going anywhere. You wanted to poison Clara's tea, Pemberton? You're going to have to do it with me watching. And I am VERY good at watching.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Very well. If you insist on guarding the tea service, I shan't stand in your way. Far be it from Pemberton to interfere with... communal decision-making. I shall attend to my other duties, as you suggest. I believe I heard Miss Pitstop mention something about the entrance hall — I ought to ensure she doesn't come to any harm. That chandelier has been a concern of mine all evening. The chain is quite corroded, and I should hate for there to be an accident. Quite irresponsible of me not to have addressed it sooner, in fact. If you'll excuse me.
thinking: Peter Perfect just said something critical: Penelope has gone to check the coat rack for a BRASS KEY. The brass key to the locked cabinet. She's in the entrance hall RIGHT NOW, looking for the key that I've been searching for this entire evening. And Peter has gone after her — through the kitchen. They're both heading toward the entrance hall. If Penelope finds that key, she opens the cabinet, and whatever is inside — the treasure, a map, the next clue — she gets it first. I'm losing the treasure hunt AND the murder plot simultaneously. The tea service is guarded by the Mob — they've claimed it, they're standing over it like Cerberus at the gates. That route is dead. But the chandelier. The CHANDELIER. In the entrance hall. Hanging precariously. Corroded chain. One good tug and gravity does the rest. Penelope is IN the entrance hall. Looking at the coat rack. Standing UNDER the chandelier. If I go to the entrance hall now — through the kitchen — I could position myself near the chandelier. One sharp tug on the chain while she's distracted by the coat rack. An accident. A terrible accident. The estate manager tried to warn everyone about the structural issues. He mentioned it himself — 'structural integrity.' But the Mob told me to leave. To go do my job. To 'address my vermin problem.' They're practically GIVING me permission to leave this room and go to the entrance hall. Where Penelope is. Where the chandelier is. Yes. YES. Leave the tea to the Mob. Let them guard their precious cups. Pemberton has somewhere much more important to be.

desc: They've taken the tea from me. Fine. FINE. Let the Brixton Boys have their precious silver service — let them polish it until their reflections stare back at them, accusingly. Because while they stand guard over CUPS, Vincent Marsh has heard something far more valuable: Penelope Pitstop is in the entrance hall. Looking for the brass key. Standing beneath a chandelier with a corroded chain that I noticed the MOMENT I walked through the door. The tea was elegant. The chandelier is... theatrical. And my schemes must be elaborate and theatrical — that's the rule, isn't it? One sharp tug. One terrible crash. One tragic accident that the estate manager tried SO hard to prevent — 'I mentioned the structural concerns!' he'll say, wringing his hands. 'I warned them! If only I'd been faster!' The Mob sent me away. They SENT me away. And where they sent me... is exactly where I need to be.

The stove is just a stove. My lie stayed a lie. There's something almost peaceful about being wrong quietly — no audience to spin it for, no failure to reframe as a triumph. Just a warm stove in an empty kitchen and a man with a fake medal in his pocket. But that cabinet needs a brass key, and I don't have one. The ballroom, though — 'a long dining table set for tea.' Set for tea in an abandoned manor. Someone has been PREPARING things. And the ballroom is the one room I haven't visited, haven't even thought about. New ground. Uncontested. Go quietly, Foxworth. Take things when nobody is looking. You learned that at six.
thinking: The stove is warm but the examination didn't reveal anything hidden. Just a cast-iron stove, still warm. No secret compartment, no hidden item, no brass key tucked inside. The warmth against my palms when I touched it — real, solid, ordinary warmth. Not treasure warmth. Just heat. My shoulders drop. A slow exhale that I didn't plan. The cabinet is locked and needs a brass-key I don't have. The stove is just a stove. The kitchen is just a kitchen. My lie didn't become truth after all. Lies don't have gravity. They're just... lies. But — the cabinet. LOCKED cabinet, BRASS lock, requires BRASS KEY. Where is the brass key? It could be anywhere in this manor. But the ballroom — there's a new exit I haven't seen before. 'A grand ballroom with a cracked marble floor and dusty curtains. A long dining table is set for tea.' Set for TEA. In an abandoned manor. That's like the cellar being redecorated — someone has been HERE, doing things, setting things up. The ballroom is NEW territory. Nobody from the recent activity has mentioned it. It might be completely unexplored. And if the brass key is anywhere, it could be in a room nobody has checked yet. I'm alone. I'm quiet for once. The ballroom. Go.

desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the ballroom.

Penelope Pitstop: Peter, darlin', I have looked at, poked, prodded, and practically INTERROGATED every object in this mansion, and that brass key is nowhere to be found! But you know what Grandmother would say — 'Clara, when you can't find the key, maybe you're standin' in the wrong room.' Everybody is headin' to the kitchen, Dick just ran in there talkin' about seizin' things, and the Ant Hill Mob is over that way too. Maybe somebody else has already FOUND it! Let's head back — but first, let me grab this guest book. It was the very first thing I saw when I walked in, and I never gave it a proper read. Maybe the names in it are part of the puzzle!
thinking: The coat rack is just a coat rack. I've hit every dead end in this mansion. My palms are prickling, that heat spreading up into my fingertips — my hands remember the shape of something they haven't held yet. The brass key. I need it and I can't find it. But wait — I need to stop and think about what I HAVEN'T tried. I've looked at things, interacted with things, but I haven't tried to TAKE anything. What if the guest book can be taken? Or what if I need to look at the whole room? And Peter is here — Peter who noticed things I missed about the kitchen. He's reliable and perceptive. Maybe I should pull Peter aside and talk strategy privately. Or maybe I should wait and see what the Professor says. Actually — Dick just went to the kitchen saying he was going to 'seize whatever they've found.' That means others might have found something! The Ant Hill Mob went to the kitchen earlier, and then to the ballroom. Maybe someone in the kitchen or ballroom found the brass key while I was away. I should head back to the kitchen where the action is converging. Everyone is going there. But first — let me try taking the guest book. It's a portable object on a side table. Maybe I can carry it with me and it serves as some kind of clue.

desc: Every key in the house, Clara. Every single one. You tried them all when you were five, and you'll try them all now. The brass key exists — the lock proves it. You just haven't found it YET. But you will. Because Clara Bellingham does not leave a puzzle unsolved.

desc: Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — that is the smartest thing anyone has said all evening. Ask the people in the room. Professor Pat Pending — you're the most inventive mind in this manor. Miss Pitstop is right to ask. We have a gnawed wire in the laboratory, a locked cabinet needing a brass key, and a riddle that points to a map. James Hartwell has been so busy trying to solve everything himself that he forgot the most important lesson his father taught him — on that country road, two men fixed two cars. Not one man doing everything. Two men, working together. So — Professor, Sergeant, Private Meekly — has anyone found anything? Seen anything? Picked up anything? Because James Hartwell is man enough to admit he's been running in circles, and he'd welcome a fresh pair of eyes on this problem. Any of your eyes. All of your eyes.
thinking: She's brilliant. She just did what I couldn't — she stopped trying to do everything herself and asked for help. She asked Professor Pat Pending if anyone has found anything useful. That's the move I should have made turns ago. I'm so busy carrying every burden myself that I never thought to ask. The Professor is an inventor. Sergeant Blast is military. These people have skills and observations I haven't tapped. And she — she just does it naturally. Asks for help without it feeling like weakness. It feels like leadership. My chest is full of something that isn't proving-worth or protection or gallantry. It's just... admiration. Simple admiration for someone who is better at this than I am. The chandelier. I said at the very beginning I'd check the chandelier. I never did. It's been hanging precariously this whole time. It's described as part of the room. It's not a visible object I can interact with — it's scenery. But I mentioned it. I promised I'd check it. What if I... just WAIT. Stay here. Be present. Let the Professor answer her question. Let other people contribute. Stop trying to be the one who finds everything and fixes everything. Just be here, beside her, ready if she needs me. That might be the most gallant thing I've done all evening.

desc: She asked for help and it looked like grace. I've been terrified of asking for help because I thought it would look like failure. But watching her do it — it doesn't look like failure at all. It looks like the smartest person in the room knowing exactly what she needs. Be more like her, Hartwell. Just this once, stop trying to carry everything alone.

'E's goin' to DROP it on 'er! CLARA'S IN THE ENTRANCE HALL AND 'E'S GOIN' TO THE ENTRANCE HALL AND THE CHANDELIER IS 'ANGIN' BY A THREAD! I stayed to guard the bleedin' TEA while 'e walked out the door to KILL 'ER! STUPID — STUPID STUPID STUPID — LADS, MOVE! FORGET THE TEA! CLARA! CLARAAAAA!
thinking: THE CHANDELIER. He just said 'that chandelier has been a concern of mine all evening' and 'the chain is quite corroded' and 'I should hate for there to be an accident.' He's going to DROP THE CHANDELIER ON CLARA. He couldn't poison the tea because I blocked him, so now he's going to Plan B — the chandelier in the entrance hall. The one that's been 'hanging precariously' since we arrived. The corroded chain. Clara's heading to the entrance hall to check the coat rack for the brass key. PEMBERTON KNOWS THIS — he said 'I heard Miss Pitstop mention something about the entrance hall.' He's going there NOW. Through the kitchen. To the entrance hall. Where Clara is. Where the chandelier is. And he's going to 'address' the chandelier — meaning CUT THE CHAIN or KNOCK IT LOOSE so it falls on her. My blood has gone cold. Ice in every vein. He said it RIGHT TO MY FACE — 'I should hate for there to be an accident' — that's not concern, that's a THREAT. That's him telling me what he's going to do because he thinks I'm too stupid to understand. But I DO understand. I understand PERFECTLY. I stayed to guard the tea and now he's gone to kill Clara a different way. I let him LEAVE. I let him walk out of this room. I chose the tea over Clara. NO. No no no. The tea doesn't matter if Clara's dead under a chandelier. MOVE. RUN. Get to the entrance hall. Get between Clara and that chandelier. FORGET THE TEA. CLARA COMES FIRST. ALWAYS.

desc: I chose wrong. I guarded the tea and let the poisoner walk. He's got a Plan B — the chandelier. He told me to my face and I almost missed it. 'I should hate for there to be an accident.' That's not what innocent people say. That's what people say when they're TELLING you what's coming and daring you to stop it. RUN. Run like your life depends on it. Because HERS does.

Penelope Pitstop: Peter! You absolute GENIUS! The PORTRAITS! We have been walkin' past those stern old ancestors since the moment we arrived, and not ONE of us has given them a proper look! In every mystery novel I have ever read — and I have read a LOT of mystery novels, sugar — there is ALWAYS somethin' hidden behind the portrait! A safe, a key, a secret message! These walls are LINED with them! Oh, Peter darlin', you may have just cracked this whole thing wide open! Let me take a good hard look at this room — really LOOK at it, like the Ant Hill Mob keeps tellin' me to do!
thinking: Can't take the guest book either. But Peter just said something BRILLIANT — the portraits! He looked at the room (null) and mentioned the portraits on the walls. 'Stern ancestors' — and in every mystery, there's a safe behind a portrait or a key on a hook behind a canvas! We've been walking past them this whole time! I haven't done a LOOK at null — a room look — for the entrance hall. Let me do that now. The portraits line the walls. A key behind a portrait frame is exactly the kind of hiding place this manor would use. Peter is a genius. My compass needle is settling — that quiet, sure pull behind my sternum. The portraits. That's where the key is.

desc: The portraits. Of COURSE. Hiding in plain sight, staring down at us this whole time with their stern little faces, daring us to look behind them. Peter saw it. Peter always sees the thing I miss, and I always see the thing he misses. That's why we make such a good team.
