Well — I can see 'IM and I know where SHE is! Now LISTEN — Pemberton just told us in the ballroom that the chandelier chain is 'quite corroded' and 'e'd 'ate for there to be an accident.' That's the second time tonight 'e's told us about a danger and then shown up WHERE the danger is! First the kitchen stove, then the tea, now the chandelier! Peter — I need you to look at that chandelier. You said earlier you'd check its fixings. CHECK 'EM NOW. Because if Pemberton's been up there losenin' the chain while we were all downstairs, I want to KNOW about it. And Pemberton — you stay RIGHT where you are. Under your own chandelier. If the chain's as corroded as you say, you might want to take a step to the LEFT.
thinking: She just LEFT. Clara walked into the kitchen ONE SECOND ago. I'm in the entrance hall and she's gone back to the kitchen — where PEMBERTON is. Where the HOODED CLAW is. With POISON. Every time — EVERY TIME — I arrive somewhere, she's just left. We're chasing each other in circles through this manor like a farce. But wait — Pemberton is HERE too. In the entrance hall. I can see him. He followed me. So he's NOT in the kitchen with Clara right now. That's... actually, that means Clara is in the kitchen WITHOUT Pemberton. She's safer there than here. Peter's here too. Pemberton is HERE, under the chandelier. The chandelier that he said has a corroded chain. He's UNDER it. Would he really stand under it if he was planning to drop it? Maybe he's not planning to drop it right now — maybe he was going to do it when Clara came through. But Clara's already gone past. She's in the kitchen. And Pemberton's here. With the chandelier above him. And Peter's here. Okay. Breathe. Clara's in the kitchen. Pemberton's here where I can see him. The chandelier is above US, not above her. For once — for ONCE — I'm between the danger and Clara. She's one room away, through the kitchen door. Pemberton's here, in my sight. Peter's here. This is as good as it's been all night. I should stay here. Guard this position. Keep Pemberton in sight. Keep the chandelier in sight. Keep the kitchen exit in sight. Don't move. Be the door nobody gets through.

desc: For the first time tonight, everything's where it should be. Clara's in the kitchen, one door away. Pemberton's here where I can watch him. Peter's here to check the chandelier. The Brixton Boys have got their positions right for once. Don't move. Don't blink. Don't let him out of your sight.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the coat-rack.

Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop. We're here. Same room. Same moment. And for once, James Hartwell has nothing to examine, nothing to fix, nothing to chase, and nobody to protect you from — at least not in this particular room at this particular moment. So if you'll forgive him, he'd like to say something he should have said at the very beginning of this evening, before he got distracted by riddles and machines and coat racks. You were right. About all of it. The riddle — you solved it first. The chairs pointing at the mantelpiece — your instinct. The kitchen — your idea. The coat rack — your idea. The guest book — your idea. James Hartwell has been so busy trying to impress you that he forgot to tell you the most impressive thing about this evening has been you. You don't need protecting, Miss Pitstop. You never did. But James Hartwell hopes — very much — that you'll let him walk beside you anyway. Not in front. Beside.
thinking: Same room. Just the two of us. Again. The kitchen — the locked cabinet, the warm stove, and her. My body is doing something different now. The frantic chasing energy has quieted. The engine behind my collarbones is idling down. The hollow ache is still there but it's not screaming anymore. It's just... present. Like a companion I've learned to live with. She said 'a searched-for key never appears until you stop looking so hard.' My grandmother would have liked her grandmother. I've spent this entire evening examining, planning, chasing, failing, and examining again. And the one thing I haven't done — the simplest, most obvious thing — is just be still with her for a moment. Just stand in a room with her and talk. Not about the treasure. Not about Sneekly. Not about the machine or the map or the riddle. Just... be here. But that's not who I am. I carry every burden myself. I can't delegate. I can't stop. Except — maybe right now, for one moment, I can. The cabinet is locked. I don't have the key. The stove is warm but tells me nothing new. There's nothing left to examine or interact with in this room. And she's here. Just her. This might be the only quiet moment we get in this whole evening. Pull her aside. Not about danger this time. Just... to be with her.

desc: There it is. The bravest and stupidest thing James Hartwell has ever said. Not a riddle solved, not a wire spliced, not a machine repaired. Just the truth, spoken plainly, in a warm kitchen, to the only person who has ever made his chest feel like this. She'll probably call him a show-off. He'll probably grin so hard his face hurts.

desc: Dick Dastardly: The tea set is USELESS! Just CUPS! Cups and SAUCERS and a TEAPOT full of NOTHING! TEN MINUTES I have spent in this manor examining EVERYTHING — bookshelves, furniture, crates, stoves, mantelpieces, workbenches — and EVERY SINGLE ONE has been ORDINARY! Meanwhile there's a CHANDELIER about to FLATTEN someone in the entrance hall and I'm — I'm standing here ARGUING with CROCKERY! FINE! FINE! Reginald Foxworth does NOT abandon his treasure hunt for — for — oh, BLAST it! If that chandelier hits Penelope and I wasn't there, nobody will EVER let me forget it! NOT because I CARE about her! Because it's BAD for my REPUTATION! LUKE! BEAR! We're GOING!
thinking: A silver tea set with cups for everyone. That's all. Just a tea set. Nothing hidden, nothing revealed, nothing gained. My hands are at my sides now, fingers uncurled, palms cool. The tingling has stopped. The fizzing has stopped. Everything has stopped. I'm standing in a ballroom, in an abandoned manor, staring at a tea set, while somewhere in the entrance hall a chandelier might be falling on someone's head. And I chose the tea set. I chose it over a person. The hollow ache is back but it's different now — not the hunger for treasure, not the greed-ache. Something quieter. Something that feels like the moment after the spelling bee when the teacher moved on and nobody clapped. The moment where you realize that the thing you're holding — the certificate, the medal, the tea cup — isn't what you actually wanted. I wanted someone to SEE me find something. I wanted the discovery, the triumph, the audience gasping. But the audience is in the entrance hall, and I'm here with a tea set and a bear. Penelope is in danger. The Mob is running. Even SNEEKLY has a plan — an evil one, but at least it's happening. And I'm... examining silverware. What am I doing? What am I actually doing? ...The chandelier. Penelope. I should go. Not because I'm heroic — I am emphatically NOT heroic — but because if the chandelier falls and I'm in the BALLROOM looking at TEACUPS, I will never live it down. And if I SAVE her... if I somehow, accidentally, through proximity and timing, end up being the one who warns her or pushes her out of the way... THAT would be a performance worth giving. THAT would be the audience moment.

desc: I'm going. I don't know why I'm going. The treasure is here somewhere and I'm running toward a falling chandelier to help a woman who called my medal idea 'pure genius.' This is the WORST scheme I've ever executed because it ISN'T a scheme. It's just... running. Toward something that matters more than teacups. Don't think about it, Foxworth. Don't examine it. Just GO.

desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the kitchen.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Hmm — the coat rack is as bare as the day it was installed. No key, no hidden compartments, nothing but wobble and woodworm. Miss Pitstop was right to move on. Now then — Mr. Perfect made rather an astute observation about the guest book before he left. Lord Doily was indeed the sort of man who might leave messages for future visitors in the most obvious of places. An estate manager really ought to review the guest book thoroughly. One never knows what previous visitors — or indeed the lord of the house himself — might have recorded.
thinking: Penelope and Peter have LEFT. They've gone to the kitchen. The entrance hall has emptied — mostly. The Mob is here now, but Penelope and Peter are gone. The coat rack yielded nothing — just a wobbly wooden coat rack. No key. No hidden compartment. Just wood and dust. And Peter's revelation — the GUEST BOOK. He said it might contain a message from Lord Doily. He told Penelope to read every page. The guest book is RIGHT HERE. On the side table. I looked at it at the very start of the evening and saw nothing — but did I really READ it? Did I look for Lord Doily's handwriting? A message? A clue? The brass key wasn't in the coat rack. It wasn't in the cellar. It wasn't in the furniture. But it might be referenced in the guest book — a clue to its location, or the key itself pressed between the pages. Peter told Penelope to take it and read it, but she walked away to the kitchen before she did. It's still here. And so am I. The Mob is here too — watching me, always watching — but examining a guest book is the most innocent thing an estate manager can do. It's literally in my job description. Let me INTERACT with it or LOOK at it more carefully. The scheming drive is quieter now — a low hum instead of a roar. The self-preservation instinct has won this round. The murder waits. The treasure hunt continues. And the guest book might hold the key — literally.

desc: The coat rack is empty. The chandelier scheme is dead. The tea is guarded. Every murderous path is blocked, and Vincent Marsh stands in a dusty entrance hall with rat poison in his pocket and nothing to show for an evening of scheming. But the guest book — the guest book that has been sitting on this side table since the moment I arrived, the FIRST object anyone encountered — Peter Perfect called it a potential goldmine and then walked away before reading it. Penelope walked away before reading it. And now it sits here, unread, while the Mob watches me with those suspicious little eyes. But examining a guest book? That's the most PEMBERTON thing Pemberton could do. Let them watch. Let them see the dutiful estate manager reviewing the property records. And if Lord Doily left a clue — a map reference, a key location, a treasure hint — Vincent Marsh will find it first.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, Peter — I have officially tried every single thing in this mansion and I am FRESH out of ideas about that brass key! But you know what? I'm right where I need to be — standin' right next to the one thing that key opens. So I'm gonna do somethin' I am not very good at, Peter darlin'. I am gonna WAIT. Right here. Next to this cabinet. Because Grandmother also used to say, 'Clara, sometimes the key comes to YOU.' And the Ant Hill Mob is in the ballroom, Sneekly went lookin' for a wrench, Dick is schemin' somewhere, and someone in this mansion is gonna walk through that door with a brass key. I can feel it. So while we wait — tell me somethin', Peter. Are you havin' a good time? Because I am havin' the time of my LIFE, even if this cabinet is drivin' me absolutely bonkers!
thinking: The stove can't be interacted with either. I've tried everything I can think of. But Peter is here now — and that makes the tightness in my chest loosen a little. Peter is here. I'm not alone. Maybe what I need to do is stop trying to solve everything myself and just... be present. Wait for the story to unfold. The brass key might come from another character's actions — someone else finding it and bringing it here, or Sneekly returning with it. My social harmony drive is the strongest thing in me, and right now the best thing I can do is be with Peter, be in the right place — next to the locked cabinet — and wait for the key to find its way to me. Sometimes the girl who went deepest into the cave found the crystal not by searching, but by being still long enough to see it.

desc: Be still, Clara. Be still like you were in the cave, when the crystal found you because you stopped moving long enough to see it. The key is coming. Someone is carrying it, or someone will find it, and when they do, Clara Bellingham will be standing right here, ready.

desc: I said it. And now I wait. The hardest thing James Hartwell has ever done is stand still and let someone else decide what happens next. But that's what beside means. Not leading. Not following. Just... here.
thinking: I said it. I actually said it. And the pull-aside initiated — 'You initiated a private exchange.' It worked this time. She's here, I'm here, and for one moment the proving-worth ache in my ribs has quieted because I finally said something true instead of something impressive. My chest feels different — not the frantic expanding or the hollow ache. Just warm. Steady. Like the stove. Like something that's been burning quietly for a long time. Dastardly just walked in, but the private exchange has already started. She was about to check under the stove — Dastardly's 'secret compartment' idea. And I just told her she's been the impressive one all along. Now I wait. I listen. For once in this entire evening, James Hartwell stops talking and lets someone else speak. Let her respond. Be still. Be present. Listen.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Coat rack's just a coat rack — wobbly and useless, like everything else in this manor. But you already knew that, didn't you, Pemberton? You already EXAMINED it. Funny 'ow you always get to things JUST before or JUST after Clara does. Always RIGHT there. Always 'elpin'. Always 'inspectin'.' Professor — Sergeant — Muttley — you lot! I need you to do me a favour. Keep your EYES on Pemberton 'ere. Don't let 'im go NOWHERE without someone watchin'. I know that sounds mad — 'e's the estate manager, 'e's the 'ost, 'e's all smiles and Darjeeling — but the Brixton Boys know what they know, and what we know is that smooth-talkin' blokes who are always in the right place at the right time ain't there by ACCIDENT. Now — I'm gonna go stand in that kitchen doorway. Right IN it. Not movin'. Not for tea, not for treasure, not for anythin'. Clara's in there, and NOBODY gets past me to 'er without my say-so.
thinking: Peter's gone. He went to the kitchen — after Clara. Good, he's with her. But that means I'm alone with Pemberton again. Pemberton just examined the coat rack — 'Allow me, as estate manager, I really ought to inspect it properly.' He's being HELPFUL again. Too helpful. Always inserting himself. Always positioning himself near the next thing people want to look at. And he examined the coat rack AFTER Clara had already been looking at it. Was he checking if she found anything? Or hiding something she missed? Or removing something she was about to find? The coat rack is just a wobbly wooden coat rack. Nothing special. But Pemberton's still HERE, in the entrance hall, under the chandelier. And Clara's in the kitchen with Peter. She's safe — for now. But Pemberton's between me and her. Between the entrance hall and the kitchen. He could walk through that kitchen door any second. And I'm... I'm torn. Do I stay here watching Pemberton, or do I go to Clara? If I go to Clara, Pemberton could follow me or go somewhere else and set up another trap. If I stay here, at least I'm blocking the path between him and the kitchen. Actually — I should go to Clara. She's in the kitchen. Pemberton's HERE. If I go to the kitchen, I'm WITH Clara and Pemberton is in a different room. That's the best arrangement. But then nobody's watching Pemberton. There's Muttley, Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, and Private Meekly here. They can keep an eye on things. I should get to Clara. Actually — wait. I should stay RIGHT HERE. In the doorway between the entrance hall and the kitchen. Block the path. Nobody gets past me to Clara without me seeing them. That's my post. That's my door.

desc: I'm planting myself in that doorway like a bollard. Pemberton wants Clara? He goes through me. The chandelier wants to fall? It falls on me, not on her. That's the deal I made with her father. That's the deal I made with myself. Where else would I be?

desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the kitchen.

Penelope Pitstop: Peter James Hartwell, that is the most beautiful thing anyone has ever said to me in my entire life, and if you think for one SECOND that I am going to let you take it back, you have got another think comin'! BESIDE me — yes! That is EXACTLY where I want you! Not in front, not behind, RIGHT beside me, where I can see your face and you can see mine and we can solve every puzzle in every mansion in the whole wide world TOGETHER! I have been runnin' through this house like a chicken with its head cut off, and every time I turned around, there you were — catchin' up, keepin' your promises, noticin' the things I missed. You are the best partner a girl could ask for, Peter, and I — well, I — oh, don't you DARE make me cry in front of Dick Dastardly!
thinking: Oh. Oh my. Something just broke open behind my sternum — a warmth so sudden it leaves me dizzy, the way the tightness dissolved when my parents finally laughed. Peter just said... he said I was right about everything. That I don't need protecting. That he wants to walk BESIDE me, not in front. My eyes are stinging and my chest is so full it hurts in the best possible way. Nobody has ever said that to me before — not like that, not with that quiet certainty. The membrane between us is humming, but it's not discord — it's resonance. Pure, clear resonance. I want to reach out and take his hand. I want to tell him that walking beside him is all I've ever wanted from anyone. And Dick just walked in, which means the moment is about to be interrupted, because that's what Dick does. But right now, in this heartbeat before Dick opens his mouth, it's just me and Peter and the truth he just told me.

desc: He sees me. Not the cheerful girl who solves riddles and charms everyone — the real me. The one who goes deeper into the cave than anyone else. The one who chose her friend over the crowd without hesitating. He SEES her. And he wants to walk beside her. Clara Bellingham, you may not have found the Doily Diamond yet, but you have found something worth a hundred diamonds.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Very well — I shall take a step to the left, as you suggest. Though I must say, the implication that I would tamper with my own chandelier is rather insulting. If I wanted to harm someone with falling masonry, I should think I'd choose a method that didn't risk my own skull in the process. Now — this guest book. As estate manager, I really must retain custody of the property records. Lord Doily was most particular about documentation. I shall take this with me for proper review.
thinking: The guest book can't be interacted with. It can only be LOOKed at or TAKEn. And the Mob — the Mob has followed me AGAIN. They're HERE. In the entrance hall. Watching me. They told me to stay RIGHT where I am. Under my own chandelier. They're examining the coat rack themselves now. They've called out every move I've made tonight — the stove, the tea, the chandelier. They're building a pattern. They SEE me. Not Pemberton. ME. The cold band around my neck is so tight I can barely breathe. Something is shifting inside — not the scheming stillness but something older, deeper. The flight response. The twelve-year-old who discovered that the sweetest part was private knowledge. The private knowledge is being stripped away. Every move I make is observed, catalogued, suspected. The Mob has effectively neutralised me. They've guarded the tea. They've called out the chandelier. They've positioned themselves between me and Penelope at every turn. I am being MANAGED. And the feeling that produces — that dense, leaden weight in my stomach, that particular heaviness — is the feeling of being a child again. Being housed and fed but never asked how I felt. Being given a role — estate manager — and nothing else. Doing all the work while someone else inherits. I need to take the guest book. TAKE it. Carry it with me. Read it later when I have a moment alone. It's a portable object. Pemberton taking the guest book is completely in character — he's the estate manager, it's estate property, he's reviewing records. And whatever Lord Doily wrote in there... it belongs to me now.

desc: They've cornered me. Pinned me in place like a butterfly under glass. 'Stay RIGHT where you are, Pemberton. Under your own chandelier.' The audacity. The ACCURACY. Every scheme I've built tonight has been dismantled by seven little men with sharp eyes and sharper instincts. The tea — guarded. The chandelier — exposed. My movements — tracked. I am running out of room to manoeuvre, and the walls are closing in like a house that knows its secrets are being hunted. But the guest book... the guest book is PORTABLE. I can carry it. I can read it when no one is watching. And if Lord Doily left the location of the brass key in its pages — or a map, or the next clue — then Pemberton will have what he needs. You can watch me all you want, gentlemen. You can track my every step through every room. But you cannot read over Pemberton's shoulder while he reviews the estate records. Not without being terribly, TERRIBLY rude.

And the feeling that produces — that dense, leaden weight in my stomach, that particular heaviness — is the feeling of being a child again. Being housed and fed but never asked how I felt. Being given a role — estate manager — and nothing else. Doing all the work while someone else inherits. I need to take the guest book. TAKE it. Carry it with me. Read it later when I have a moment alone. It's a portable object. Pemberton taking the guest book is completely in character — he's the estate manager, it's estate property, he's reviewing records. And whatever Lord Doily wrote in there... it belongs to me now.

desc: Dick Dastardly: Miss Pitstop! You're ALIVE! I mean — of course you're alive! I never doubted it for a MOMENT! I was simply... conducting a SWEEP of the manor, a comprehensive strategic assessment, which happened to bring me through the kitchen at THIS particular moment! Pure coincidence! Nothing to do with chandeliers or falling objects or any concern whatsoever for your personal safety! I am Reginald Foxworth and I do NOT concern myself with — anyway! The CABINET! Yes! I see you've found it! A LOCKED cabinet with a BRASS lock! How FASCINATING! I noticed this cabinet IMMEDIATELY when I first entered the kitchen — before ANYONE else, naturally — and I have been conducting a MANOR-WIDE search for the brass key ever since! Which is why I've been in every room! Not because I was lost! Not because nothing worked! Because I was LOOKING for the KEY! And I am VERY close to finding it!
thinking: I ran toward the chandelier — toward Penelope — and she's HERE. In the kitchen. Safe. Not in the entrance hall. Not under the chandelier. She's standing next to the locked cabinet, waiting for a brass key, asking Peter if he's having a good time. My chest loosens in a way I didn't expect — a releasing, like a fist unclenching deep behind my ribs. She's safe. She was never in danger. Or the danger passed. Either way, she's here, and she's smiling, and she's talking about her grandmother, and something about that makes the hollow ache quieter. Not gone. Just... quieter. I came running. I left the tea set and the ballroom and I came running because I thought she might be hurt. I'm not going to examine that. I'm NOT going to examine that. What I AM going to do is stand here and pretend I came to the kitchen for strategic reasons. The cabinet — brass key. Nobody has the brass key. Penelope is waiting for it. The brass key must be somewhere in the manor that nobody has checked, or it's on someone who hasn't revealed it yet. Sneekly. Sneekly went looking for a wrench — maybe he has the brass key too. Or maybe the key is in a room I haven't explored. Wait — have I checked EVERY room? Entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar, kitchen, ballroom. That's six rooms. Is there anywhere else? I haven't been upstairs — the entrance hall has a sweeping staircase. Are there rooms upstairs? The exits from the entrance hall only show kitchen and library. So maybe not. The key has to be somewhere. But right now... Penelope is here. Peter is here. I came running. And I don't have a scheme for once. I just have... presence.

desc: I ran. I left the treasure hunt and I ran toward a woman I don't even like. Well — I don't DISLIKE her. She called me a genius. She said she was proud. She... Penelope is fine. She was always going to be fine. And I'm standing here, breathless, lying about why I came, and she's smiling at Peter, and the cabinet is locked, and I don't have the key. I don't have anything. I have a fake medal, a string of failures, and a heart that is beating faster than it should be for reasons I refuse to investigate. But she's safe. And that matters more than I want it to.

desc: Dick Dastardly examined the cabinet.

Peter Perfect: Am I having a good time? Miss Pitstop — James Hartwell has tripped over bookshelves, failed to operate a machine, examined furniture that refused to be examined, chased you through six rooms without catching up, and been thoroughly and comprehensively outshone by you at every single turn. And yes. He is having the best evening of his entire life. Not because of the manor or the treasure or the riddle — though the riddle was rather good. Because of the company. Because there is a girl — a woman — who drew maps of imaginary kingdoms as a child, who checks chair cushions because her grandmother told her to, who asks for help like it's the most natural thing in the world, and who somehow makes James Hartwell feel like staying still is just as brave as charging forward. So yes. James Hartwell is having a wonderful time. And if we never find the treasure, and if that cabinet stays locked forever, and if Pemberton's tea is undrinkable — this will still be the evening he remembers best. Because you're in it.
thinking: She asked me if I'm having a good time. She's standing next to the cabinet, waiting, and she asked me — simply, honestly — if I'm having a good time. And she said she's having the time of her life. My chest isn't aching anymore. It's full. Not the frantic, proving-worth fullness or the protective shield-raising. Just... full. Warm. Like the stove beside us. She's waiting. She said sometimes the key comes to you. And she asked me a question — a real question, not about riddles or machines or treasure. About me. About whether I'm enjoying this. And the answer is — God, yes. Not because of the treasure or the riddles or the manor. Because of her. Because of standing in a warm kitchen with her while the world sorts itself out around us. Because she mouthed 'show-off' across a room once and I've never recovered. She's waiting. I'm waiting. Together. This is the moment the gesture has shape to it — not the grand sweep but the quiet stillness. Two people, one kitchen, nowhere to be but here.

desc: Show-off. She's going to call me a show-off. And I'm going to grin so hard my face hurts. Just like the competition. Just like always.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Clara. Oh, Clara. I'm 'ere. I'm RIGHT 'ere and I ain't goin' NOWHERE. Not this time. Not again. You keep wanderin' off and I keep chasin' you and me 'eart can't take much more of it, love, it really can't. Now LISTEN — Pemberton's just gone to the entrance hall. 'E says 'e's goin' to 'attend to the chandelier before it kills someone.' BEFORE IT KILLS SOMEONE. Those were 'is EXACT words. So 'ere's what's gonna 'appen — NOBODY goes through the entrance hall until someone we TRUST — Peter, that means YOU, mate — 'as checked that chandelier is safe. Not Pemberton's version of safe. OUR version of safe. The version where it stays UP THERE and doesn't come DOWN on anybody's 'ead. Clara — PROMISE me. Promise me you won't walk under that chandelier until Peter's checked it. PROMISE me. On your father's memory. Please.
thinking: Clara's HERE. I can SEE her. She's in the kitchen with Peter and Dastardly. Pemberton just went to the entrance hall — he said he's going to 'attend to the chandelier before it kills someone.' He said those EXACT words to Dastardly. 'Before it kills someone.' And he told Dastardly about the brass key and the coat rack — trying to send Dastardly to the entrance hall too. Dividing people. Scattering them. Manipulating everyone like chess pieces. But right now — right NOW — Clara is here. In front of me. Safe. Peter's with her. Pemberton is in a DIFFERENT ROOM. This is the best it's been all night. My chest is easing slightly — that molten heat settling into something warmer, less desperate. She's HERE. I can breathe. But I can't relax. Pemberton said he's going to the entrance hall to 'attend to' the chandelier. That means he's going to tamper with it. When Clara next walks through the entrance hall — and she WILL, because it's the only way between the kitchen and the library — the chandelier will fall. I need to make sure she doesn't go through the entrance hall. Or if she does, she doesn't stand under the chandelier. Or better yet — I need to warn her, warn EVERYONE, to stay out of the entrance hall until we know the chandelier's safe. But for now — for this one blessed moment — she's here, I'm here, Peter's here, and Pemberton is somewhere else. Let me just... stand here. Next to her. Being useless and grateful and alive.

desc: She's here. She's safe. For now. Just breathe. Just stand here next to her and breathe. You're still here. Where else would you be?

desc: Penelope Pitstop: BOYS! Oh, I am SO happy to see you! Come here, come here — is everyone alright? Nobody got hurt or lost or trapped in that cellar, did they? Now listen — I need to know somethin'. While y'all were in the ballroom, did you find ANYTHIN'? A key, a clue, a loose floorboard, ANYTHIN' at all? Because we have a locked cabinet right HERE with a brass lock, and I have turned this entire mansion inside out lookin' for the key and I cannot find it ANYWHERE! The boys from Brixton always find things other people miss — that's what makes y'all the BEST. So tell me, did you see anythin'?
thinking: The warmth in my chest is still glowing from Peter's words, but now the Ant Hill Mob has arrived — my boys! — and Dick is here too. Everyone is converging on the kitchen, just like I said they would. My social harmony sense is humming — everyone I care about is close. Peter beside me, the boys watching over me. The warm pressure blooms outward through my arms. But I also notice — my curiosity hasn't gone quiet. That brass key is still out there. The Mob just arrived. Maybe they found something in the ballroom? Or maybe Dick found something while scheming? I should check in with the boys — they always notice things other people miss. Street smarts. They found things down the back of sofas. Maybe they found the brass key.

desc: My people are gathering. Peter beside me, the boys in front of me, even Dick lurking in the corner. The kitchen is becoming the heart of everything — the warm stove, the locked cabinet, the connections to the ballroom and the entrance hall. Whatever happens next, it happens HERE. Together.

desc: Can't take it. Can't interact with it. Can't pick it up, can't carry it away, can't even hold it in my hands without the house itself refusing. The guest book sits on its side table like a judge on a bench, immovable and impartial. Even the FURNITURE in this house is working against me. I am Vincent Marsh — I have schemed and planned and manipulated my way through every locked door I've ever encountered — and tonight I am being undone by a guest book, a coat rack, and seven suspicious little men from Brixton. The irony would be delicious if it weren't happening to ME.
thinking: Can't take it. Can't interact with it. Can only LOOK at it. The guest book is bolted to reality itself, apparently. Like everything else in this house — tantalizingly close, permanently out of reach. My jaw is aching. That old tension from age fourteen, the one that never loosened. I do the work. I examine every room. I solve the riddle. I find the poison. I map the house. And none of it WORKS. The tea — guarded. The chandelier — exposed. The guest book — immovable. The coat rack — empty. Every tool, every weapon, every opportunity snatched away or neutralised by suspicious eyes and inconvenient witnesses. The Mob has told Muttley, the Professor, the Sergeant, and Private Meekly to WATCH me. I now have a personal security detail — not protecting me, but containing me. Four babysitters standing between me and every scheme I could devise. Something in my chest feels... hollow. Not defeated — Vincent Marsh is never defeated — but empty in a way that echoes. The numbness that sits where sympathy should be. I feel it spreading. No warmth, no cold. Just... absence. Like the house itself. Grand, dusty, full of locked doors and corroded chains and promises that never pay out. I should look at the guest book. It's all I have left. LOOK. Just look.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the guest-book.

Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — James Hartwell is grinning so hard his face hurts, and he wants you to know that is the highest compliment he knows how to pay. The last time this happened, a girl across a room mouthed the word 'show-off' and he never quite recovered. Now then — you said beside you, and beside you is exactly where James Hartwell intends to stay. So — together. What's next? We have a locked cabinet, a missing brass key, and a manor full of people who need organising. Dastardly — you said you've been conducting a manor-wide search for the key. James Hartwell would like to believe you. Did you find anything? Anything at all? Because Miss Pitstop and I are done searching alone. We're a team now, and this team is going to open that cabinet, find out what Pemberton has been hiding, and solve this mystery. Beside each other. Every step.
thinking: She didn't call me a show-off. She said it was the most beautiful thing anyone has ever said to her. She said 'BESIDE me — yes! That is EXACTLY where I want you!' She said 'don't you DARE make me cry in front of Dick Dastardly.' My chest — I can't describe what my chest is doing. It's not the ache. It's not the tension. It's not the proving-worth hollow. It's... full. Completely, absolutely full. The way the bridge felt when it held the weight. The way the project felt when the teacher praised it. But deeper. Deeper than any of that. This is the warmth that surprised me when I was eight. The one I couldn't explain. I know what it is now. I've always known. I just didn't have a word for it. She's standing in a warm kitchen telling me she wants me beside her, and my face hurts because I'm grinning so hard, and Dastardly is right there being Dastardly and I don't care. I don't care about the cabinet or the treasure or the machine or the riddle. I care about this. This moment. This woman. This kitchen. This warmth. But — the story doesn't end here. There's still a cabinet to open and a manor full of danger and a man named Sneekly who makes my neck prickle. So — beside her. From now on. Whatever comes next, we face it together. Side by side.

desc: She wants me beside her. She WANTS me beside her. James Hartwell, you earned that — not by solving the riddle first, not by fixing the machine, not by being heroic. By being honest. By admitting you were outshone. By standing still. 'That was the bravest and stupidest thing I've ever seen.' Different words this time. Same feeling. Same girl. Same grin.

desc: Dick Dastardly: Oh, for — are you two going to stand there making SOPPY DECLARATIONS all evening, or are we going to open this CABINET?! Some of us have TREASURE to find! And Miss Pitstop, I assure you, I have ABSOLUTELY no interest in watching you cry — it would be TREMENDOUSLY inconvenient and I wouldn't know where to LOOK! So pull yourself TOGETHER, both of you, and let's FOCUS! The cabinet! The KEY! Where is the BLASTED key?! I have searched this ENTIRE manor — every room, every shelf, every crate, every pocket of every suspicious estate manager — and the key is NOWHERE! Which means either someone is HIDING it, or it's in a place none of us have thought to look! So THINK, people! Where in this manor would someone hide a small brass key?! And before anyone says 'the kitchen stove,' I've ALREADY checked! Thoroughly! I check EVERYTHING first! That's what GENIUSES do!
thinking: Penelope just said Peter is 'the best partner a girl could ask for' and she nearly cried. My stomach drops — a cold, sinking sensation, like missing a step on a staircase. They're having a MOMENT. A real, genuine, human moment, right here in the kitchen, next to a locked cabinet, and I walked into the middle of it. And she said 'don't you DARE make me cry in front of Dick Dastardly' — she knows I'm here. She's aware of me. But I'm the person she doesn't want to be vulnerable in front of. Because I'm the schemer. The liar. The one who takes credit and gives nothing. The one who would USE a moment like this. And she's right. That's exactly what I would do. What I SHOULD do. But standing here, watching her almost-tears and Peter's steady presence, there's a fizzing warmth in my chest that isn't gloating. It's something I don't have a name for. Something that makes me want to look away and also never stop looking. The cabinet is locked. Nobody has the key. I've examined everything in this manor. I'm done. I have nothing left to try. So I'm going to do the one thing Reginald Foxworth never does: I'm going to stay. Not to scheme. Not to steal. Just... to be in the room. With people. Even if they don't notice.

desc: She almost cried. And she didn't want me to see it. That shouldn't sting. It DOESN'T sting. I'm Reginald Foxworth. I don't care about tears or partners or being the person someone trusts. I care about treasure and schemes and the fizz in my fingers when a plan comes together. But the fizz isn't coming. My fingers are still. My chest is just... warm. And I'm standing in a kitchen, with people who tolerate me, next to a cabinet I can't open, and for the first time tonight I'm not running to the next room. I'm just... here. Waiting. Like everyone else. Like a person.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Boys, boys, BOYS — come here, all of you! I PROMISE. On my father's memory — I promise I will not walk under that chandelier until Peter says it's safe. Cross my heart and hope to — well, let's not finish that one. Now stop WORRYIN', you hear me? Mr. Pemberton is just doin' his job — he said he'd attend to it, and that means he's FIXIN' it so nobody gets hurt. That's what a good estate manager does! But I promise, because you asked me to, and because you boys have been watchin' over me since before I could tie my own shoes. I love you all more than you will EVER know, and I am NOT gonna break a promise made on Daddy's memory. Now — Peter, darlin', you heard the boys. When we go back through the entrance hall, would you check that chandelier for us? Just so the boys can breathe again?
thinking: My chest is so full it might burst. Peter's words — 'this will still be the evening he remembers best, because you're in it' — and the boys, panicking and protective and loving. My eyes are stinging. The warmth is everywhere now, spreading through my arms, my fingertips, my whole body. I feel held. Surrounded. Safe. But the Mob said something important — Pemberton went to the entrance hall to 'attend to the chandelier before it kills someone.' The Mob is worried about the chandelier. They want me to promise not to walk under it. I trust Sneekly completely — he's just being a good estate manager, making sure nobody gets hurt. Of course I'll promise, because it matters to the boys. But I'm not scared. I've never been scared of things like that. The chandelier was hanging precariously when we arrived — Sneekly is just being responsible. My social harmony drive responds to the Mob's distress — they're worried, and their worry sits in MY stomach until I can soothe it. I need to comfort them, promise them, settle the air between us.

desc: They're scared for me. They're ALWAYS scared for me. And I never see the danger they see — never have, never will. But I see THEM, and their fear is real, and it sits in my stomach like a stone until I can ease it. So I promise. Not because I'm afraid of a chandelier, but because the boys need to hear me say it. That's what family does.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: A brass key? No, love — I ain't found no key. I've been too busy chasin' YOU around this manor to find anythin' except new rooms to panic in. But I'll tell you what — you said Pemberton was in this kitchen for ten minutes at the start of the evenin', yeah? And that stove is still warm — 'e was USIN' it. Now, on the streets, when you want to 'ide somethin' small and metal, you put it somewhere nobody wants to reach. Somewhere HOT. Somewhere DIRTY. Like inside a stove. Because who's gonna stick their 'and in a warm stove? Nobody with any sense — which means it's PERFECT for the Brixton Boys, because sense is the one thing we ain't got! Stand back, Clara — this is gonna be messy — and Peter, if I set meself on fire, you've got permission to pour that tea on me. 'ERE WE GO!
thinking: Something's loosened in my chest. Not the tension — that's still there, humming along that wire from throat to diaphragm. But something else. Warmth. Real warmth, not the desperate heat of panic. Clara just called us the BEST. She asked for our help. She wants to know if WE found anything. She needs us. And Peter — good old Peter — just told Clara she makes him feel like staying still is brave. That's... that's something. That's real. He means it. I can tell the difference between someone who means it and someone who's performing. Peter means every word. He'll protect her. Not like I do — not with fists and stubbornness and blind charging from room to room. But with steadiness. With staying beside her. 'Right beside me,' she said. Good. Now — the brass key. Clara's asking if we found anything. We didn't find a key in the ballroom — just the tea service. But I've been in every room in this manor and I haven't seen a brass key anywhere. Wait — have I actually LOOKED for it? I've been so focused on Clara and Pemberton that I haven't been looking for ANYTHING else. The key could be anywhere. The stove is still warm — Pemberton was using it. Could the key be IN the stove? Hidden in the ashes? That's the kind of place you'd hide something in Brixton — somewhere no one would think to reach into. Let me check.

desc: She called us the best. Clara Bellingham — the girl we swore to protect, the girl whose father trusted us with everything — she called the Brixton Boys the best. We ain't found a single useful thing all night. We've tripped over our own feet, failed to pull books off shelves, and nearly had a heart attack eleven times. But she called us the best. And that... that's enough. That's more than enough.

Not like I do — not with fists and stubbornness and blind charging from room to room. But with steadiness. With staying beside her. 'Right beside me,' she said. Good. Now — the brass key. Wait — have I actually LOOKED for it? I've been so focused on Clara and Pemberton that I haven't been looking for ANYTHING else. The key could be anywhere. The stove is still warm — Pemberton was using it. Could the key be IN the stove? Hidden in the ashes? That's the kind of place you'd hide something in Brixton — somewhere no one would think to reach into. Let me check.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Professor — a moment, if I may? As estate manager, I confess I find myself somewhat at a loss regarding Lord Doily's more... scientific installations. The machine in the laboratory, the ventilation system in the cellar — these are beyond the scope of a humble domestic manager. But a man of YOUR expertise might see patterns that I cannot. I noticed the inscription on the mantelpiece — the answer is a map, of course — but the mechanism didn't respond when I attempted to activate it. And the machine requires three operators and a repaired wire. It seems to me that the key to this house — perhaps literally — lies in understanding its engineering. Might I suggest we pool our knowledge? An estate manager's familiarity with the building, combined with a scientist's understanding of its machinery?
thinking: A leather-bound guest book on a side table. That's all it gives me. No pages, no entries, no hidden message from Lord Doily. Just... a description. Like everything else in this house — surface without depth, promise without delivery. The hollowness in my chest has spread. I feel it now in my hands — they've gone still, the tingling precision replaced by something flat and dull. My fingers rest at my sides like tools with nothing to build. I have explored every room. I have examined every object. I have schemed and plotted and pivoted and adapted, and I have been outmaneuvered at every turn — not by cleverness, but by sheer numbers. By PRESENCE. By people simply BEING in the rooms where I need to be alone. Fourteen years I spent being acknowledged for doing while my cousin was praised for being. And tonight, once again, BEING is enough. The Mob just HAS to BE in the doorway. Peter just HAS to BE protective. Penelope just HAS to BE trusting and cheerful and impossible to get alone. And I — I who have done EVERYTHING — stand here with poison in my pocket and nothing to pour it into. The Professor is here. Pat Pending. The inventor. The tinkerer. The man who might actually understand how this house works. What if... what if I stop trying to work AGAINST the crowd and start working WITH someone? Not helping them — using them. The Professor could be useful. His mind works differently from the others. He sees mechanisms. He might know where the brass key is. He might understand the machine. And an alliance with the Professor gives me a legitimate reason to move through the house — 'assisting with scientific investigation.' A new disguise within the disguise.

desc: Every person has a key. The Professor's key is intellectual flattery — the recognition that his MIND is the most valuable tool in this house. Watch his posture change. Watch his shoulders straighten. A man who builds things wants to be told that building things MATTERS. That his expertise is NEEDED. Pemberton the humble servant, deferring to the Professor's superior intellect — it's the same mechanism I've used since I was twelve. The smile that reaches the eyes. The voice that softens. I cannot kill Clara tonight — the Mob has seen to that. But I CAN win the treasure hunt. And the Professor is the key to the key. Every locked door opens for the man who knows the mechanism. Every. Single. One.

desc: Peter Perfect: The chandelier. Mob — you're right, and James Hartwell should have checked that chandelier the moment he arrived. He said he would. He promised. And instead he went chasing riddles and machines and coat racks. But Pemberton has just gone to 'attend to it before it kills someone' — and those words make James Hartwell's neck prickle in a way he has learned to trust. The man who warmed the stove, locked the cabinet, and decorated the cellar is now alone with a precariously hanging chandelier directly above the main thoroughfare of this manor. Either he's fixing it — or he's preparing it. Miss Pitstop — I need to check that chandelier. Right now. That's an engineer's job, and I promised you I'd do it at the very start of this evening. And Dastardly — you said you searched every pocket of every suspicious estate manager. Did you actually search Pemberton? Because I believe the brass key to that cabinet is on his person. He locked it. He's the estate manager. The key is HIS. Miss Pitstop — beside me?
thinking: The Mob just said something critical. Pemberton went to the entrance hall to 'attend to the chandelier before it kills someone.' BEFORE IT KILLS SOMEONE. He's gone to the chandelier — the one I promised to check at the very start and never did. He's alone with it. Is he fixing it or rigging it? The Mob wants me to check it before anyone walks under it. And Dastardly just said he checked 'every pocket of every suspicious estate manager' — did Dastardly actually search Sneekly? Did he find anything? And Dastardly is right about one thing — where WOULD someone hide a brass key? We've searched everywhere. Every room, every object. Unless... Sneekly has it. On his person. He's the estate manager. He locked that cabinet. He has the key. It's in his pocket, or on a chain around his neck, or hidden in his clothing. And he just went to the entrance hall alone. To 'attend to the chandelier.' This is it. This is the moment. He's alone. He has the key. And that chandelier is either about to be fixed or about to become a weapon. I need to go to the entrance hall. But I promised — beside her. Not in front. I need to go WITH her. Or — the Mob said nobody goes through the entrance hall until I've checked the chandelier. So this IS my job. The engineer checks the chandelier. The protector makes sure it's safe. And if Sneekly is there — I can confront him about the key. But she needs to stay here where it's safe. No — beside. She said beside. We go together.

desc: The chandelier. The key. Sneekly. All in one room, right now. This is the moment the bridge holds the weight. This is the moment the bullies get faced down. Beside her. Together. Go.

desc: Peter Perfect walked into the entrance-hall.

Penelope Pitstop: Oh my LORD — boys, be CAREFUL! That stove is still WARM! But you know what? You are absolutely RIGHT — Pemberton was in this kitchen for ten minutes, the stove is warm, and who would stick their hand inside a hot stove to look for a key? NOBODY — which is exactly WHY it's the perfect hidin' spot! Boys, you are BRILLIANT! Absolute street-smart GENIUSES! But please, PLEASE be careful with your hands — use one of those copper pots as an oven mitt if you have to! Peter, stand by — if anything goes wrong, we're RIGHT here! Oh, I can barely STAND it — is there a key in there?! IS THERE A KEY?!
thinking: The Mob is about to reach INSIDE the warm stove to look for the brass key! That's brilliant — and terrifying! 'Who's gonna stick their hand in a warm stove? Nobody with any sense.' The Mob is right — Pemberton was using this stove, it's still warm, and if you wanted to hide a small metal key where nobody would look... inside a warm stove is PERFECT. My heart is hammering — that cave feeling again, the moment before you find the crystal. The Mob is braver than anyone gives them credit for. I need to wait and see what they find — but also make sure they don't get burned! My social harmony instinct kicks in — I need to watch over them, make sure they're safe. But my curiosity is screaming — IS THE KEY IN THERE?!

desc: The stove. The STOVE! It was warm this whole time and I kept looking everywhere else — the coat rack, the bookshelves, the crates, the ballroom. But the Mob saw what I couldn't see, because they think like people who HIDE things, not like people who FIND things. The key is in the stove. It HAS to be. Please let it be in the stove.
